    Important Words
    • viśiṣṭāḥ — especially powerful, distinguished
      From *vi-śiṣ* — to distinguish, to set apart. The same root as *Viśiṣṭa-advaita*, *Vaiśiṣṭya*. Duryodhana needs his men *distinguished* from the long enemy list he has just recited; the rhetorical move is almost visible.
    • nibodha — just take note, be informed
      Imperative of *ni-budh* — to attend, to fully apprehend. Same root as *Buddha*. Duryodhana, addressing his guru, uses an imperative of *attention* — implicitly placing himself in the teacher's chair. A reversal Vyāsa wants us to feel.
    • dvija - uttama — O best of the brāhmaṇas
      *Dvija* — twice-born — is the brāhmaṇa's proper title (initiated by the sacred thread, so *born* a second time). Duryodhana, a kṣatriya, addresses his teacher with full brāhmaṇical respect — flattery from a man whose actions consistently contradict the title's weight.
    • nāyakāḥ — captains, leaders
      From *nī* — to lead. Same root as *neta*, *vinayaka*, *nāyaka*. A leader is one who *takes others somewhere*. Duryodhana's *nāyakas* — Bhīṣma, Karṇa, Droṇa — will all be leading their men to death within eighteen days.
    • saṁjñā - artham — for information
      *Saṁjñā* (knowledge, identification) + *artham* (for the purpose of) — "for the sake of recognition." Duryodhana's whole speech is *for recognition*. He needs Droṇa to *recognize* the team he is committed to. It is a request for affirmation disguised as a briefing.
    But for your information, O best of the brāhmaṇas, let me tell you about the captains who are especially qualified to lead my military force.

    7. O best of the brāhmaṇas, understand who is on our side, the commanders of my army. I will list them so you can completely understand.
    Commentary

    Understand (nibodha) who is on our side. I will tell you in order that you completely understand (saṁjṣārtham). The word is analyzed as samyak (complete), jṣāna (knowledge).

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    7. O best of the brāhmaṇas, understand who is on our side, the commanders of my army. I will list them so you can completely understand.
    Commentary

    Thinking that Droṇa might perceive that he was fearful of the Pāṇḍavas’ army, Duryodhana then spoke boldly to cover his inner fears. “Among our troops, understand those who are particularly outstanding (viśiṣṭā), the leaders (nāyakā) endowed with great intelligence and other qualities. I will speak so that you will completely understand about them (saṁjṣānartham). If you will not fight out of affection for the Pāṇḍavas, then I will still gain victory through Bhīṣma and others.” He makes a hint of this in order to arouse the anger of Droṇa.

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Duryodhana is in a little bit of a difficult situation here, because is has three very heavy personalities on his side: Dronacarya, Bhisma and Karna. Karna did not get along with Bhisma and Drona. Bhisma was the most powerful of the warriors but he was a ksatriya, and Dronacarya was a brahmana. If Duryodhana would mention Bhisma first, Dronacarya would become very insulted and would not use all his strength in the fighting. If he mention Dronacarya first then Bhisma might feel insulted too. But since Dronacarya was a brahmana then Bhisma would accept his being mentioned first. But that would not happen if he had mentioned Karna first. Karna would be happy but the other two would be furious. So, very expertly, Duryodhana said: 'bhavan bhismas...'

    Study Notes — Gauranga Priya Dāsa
    Gauranga Priya Dāsa Study
    Bhakti-śāstrī Notes, ISKCON Chowpatty (2009)
    Theme

    COMMON THEME: Duryodhana’s actions are described – They reveal his diplomacy and inner fear by the

    following indications:

    1. Duryodhana although mentioned as king, goes to the commander on account of seriousness of

    situation – quite fit to be a politician (1.2)

    2. Points out Drona’s mistake (of imparting military secrets to son of Drupada, Dhrstadyumna who was

    born to kill Dronacharya) to make him alert and uncompromising and warns that leniency would lead to

    defeat (1.3*)

    3. Mentions great heros equal to Bhima and Arjuna (1.4*)

    Why he compares them to Bhima and Arjuna –
    Because he knew the strength of Bhima and Arjuna
    Why he mentions other heros –
    Because they were great stumbling blocks on the path of victory as each and every one of them was as formidable and Bhima and Arjuna

    4. Mentions heros who are ready to lay down their lives for “me” (like Jayadratha, Krtavarma, Salya) (1.9)

    5. Praises Bhisma – He was confident of full support of Bhismadeva and Dronacarya because:

    They did not protect Draupadi when she was insulted
    Although Bhisma and Drona have affection for Pandavas and might become lenient, he hoped that they will give up all affection now (1.11)

    6. Asks for everyone’s support for Bhisma (1.11) – because

    Bhismadeva was undoubtedly the great hero, but he was an old man and the enemy might take advantage of his full engagement on one side
    He wanted everyone to feel important
    Focus of Learning

    PLEASE NOTE: Some points of these purports are covered under the main theme above

    (a) Why Sanjaya described Duryodhana’s actions first –

    Because Dhrtarashtra was blind from birth and also bereft of spiritual vision and he knew that his sons were equally blind in the matter of religion
    And Dhrtarashtra was afraid that under the influence of the place of pilgrimage, his sons may make some compromise

    (b) Study names of warriors on both sides (1.4 – 1.9)

    (c) Duryodhana compared Bhisma (more experienced general) to Bhima (less experienced general)

    (1.10*)

    Because Duryodhana knew if he should die at all he would be killed by Bhima and was therefore always envious of Bhima
    Bhima is like a fig in the presence of Bhisma

    (d) What made Duryodhana confident of victory (1.7 – 1.11)

    Above mentioned strength of his friends (1.7 – 1.9)
    Presence of Bhisma, a far superior General than Bhima – He clearly felt that victory of Kurus dependent on the presence of Bhismadeva (1.11)
    Confident of full support of Bhisma and Drona as they had shown during Draupadi’s insulting episode (1.11 purport)
    SUBSECTION B — SIGNS OF VICTORY OF PANDAVAS (1.12* — 1.20)

    COMMON THEME: Sanjaya tactfully informed Dhrtarashtra about “his hopeless plans to win” by giving the

    following indications and signs:

    SIGNS OF VICTORY OF PANDAVAS (9 points) 1. Krishna’s personal presence confirms victory
    Supreme Personality of Godhead is the charioteer (1.14) – “jayas tu pandu-putranam yesam…”
    Krishna as Hrsikesha directly controls the senses of a pure devotee

    2. Goddess of fortune

    Whenever and wherever the Lord is present, the goddess of fortune is also there
    She never lives without her husband; therefore all fortune is guaranteed (1.14)

    3. Venue

    Kurukshetra is a holy place (1.1)

    4. Hanumanji on Arjuna’s flag

    Hanumanji also helped Lord Rama in gaining victory (1.20)

    5. Symbol of Vishnu

    Conchshell is a symbol of Vishnu (1.12* & 1.14)
    This is indirectly indicated by Bhisma and Pandavas conchshells

    6. Transcendental conchshells

    Krishna and Arjuna’s conchshell mentioned as divya (transcendental) (1.14)

    7. Bhisma’s conchshell to pacify Duryodhana (1.12*)

    8. Agnideva’s Chariot given to Arjuna

    It was capable of conquering all directions (1.14)

    9. Shattering of hearts

    Conchshells of Pandavas shattered Kauravas hearts (1.19)
    Pandavas hearts not shattered – because of confidence in Krishna
    Classical Ācāryas
    Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Classical
    Translation
    1.7 Sri Sankaracharya did not comment on this sloka. The commentary starts from 2.10.
    Śrī Rāmānujācārya Classical
    Translation
    1.1 - 1.19 Dhrtarastra said - Sanjaya said Duryodhana, after viewing the forces of Pandavas protected by Bhima, and his own forces protected by Bhisma conveyed his views thus to Drona, his teacher, about the adeacy of Bhima's forces for conering the Kaurava forces and the inadeacy of his own forces for victory against the Pandava forces. He was grief-stricken within. Observing his (Duryodhana's) despondecny, Bhisma, in order to cheer him, roared like a lion, and then blowing his conch, made his side sound their conchs and kettle-drums, which made an uproar as a sign of victory. Then, having heard that great tumult, Arjuna and Sri Krsna the Lord of all lords, who was acting as the charioteer of Arjuna, sitting in their great chariot which was powerful enough to coner the three worlds; blew their divine conchs Srimad Pancajanya and Devadatta. Then, both Yudhisthira and Bhima blew their respective conchs separately. That tumult rent asunder the hearts of your sons, led by Duryodhana. The sons of Dhrtarastra then thought, 'Our cause is almost lost now itself.' So said Sanjaya to Dhrtarastra who was longing for their victory. Sanjaya said to Dhrtarastra: Then, seeing the Kauravas, who were ready for battle, Arjuna, who had Hanuman, noted for his exploit of burning Lanka, as the emblem on his flag on his chariot, directed his charioteer Sri Krsna, the Supreme Lord-who is overcome by parental love for those who take shelter in Him who is the treasure-house of knowledge, power, lordship, energy, potency and splendour, whose sportive delight brings about the origin, sustentation and dissolution of the entire cosmos at His will, who is the Lord of the senses, who controls in all ways the senses inner and outer of all, superior and inferior - by saying, 'Station my chariot in an appropriate place in order that I may see exactly my enemies who are eager for battle.'

    Personal Guidance
    Sober self-knowledge — knowing one's own resources, allies, and limits — is essential to acting in dharma.
    Practical Applications
    • Take ten minutes to honestly inventory your spiritual resources: guru, books, devotee friends, sādhana time.
    • Identify one weakness you have been hiding from your guide; bring it forward.
    • Acknowledge one strength you have been refusing to claim out of false humility.
    Reflection Questions
    • What am I pretending not to know about my own situation?
    • Where does my self-assessment differ from how Kṛṣṇa would describe me?
    Analogy

    When a man begins a speech with "but for *your* information, let me tell you about *my* people," the pronoun-shift has already revealed the speaker's anxiety. Duryodhana turns from listing enemies to naming allies the way a gambler suddenly counts his own chips after staring too long at the table.

    Important Words
    • bhavān — your good self
      Honorific third-person pronoun — *bhavān* — addressing the teacher with the highest formal respect. Note: Duryodhana addresses Droṇa as *bhavān*, but he gave him orders one verse ago (*paśya, nibodha*). The honorific is a glove on the same hand.
    • bhīṣmaḥ — Grandfather Bhīṣma
      *Bhīṣma* — "terrible, awesome" — the name given to Devavrata after his terrifying vow of celibacy. The man's *real* name is forgotten; his vow has become his identity. The Kuru elder is, in the deepest sense, his own promise.
    • karṇaḥ — Karṇa
      Born to Kuntī before her marriage, Karṇa is — unknown to Duryodhana — the elder brother of the Pāṇḍavas. Duryodhana proudly lists his closest friend without knowing he is naming an unacknowledged Pāṇḍava. The tragedy of the *Mahābhārata* compressed into one syllable.
    • samitim - jayaḥ — always victorious in battle
      *Samiti* (assembly, battle) + *jaya* (victory) — "victor in every engagement." An honorific applied here to Kṛpa (and by extension to the elders). The Gītā will redefine *jaya* later as inner mastery; here it still means external winning. The whole text will pull the word inward.
    • aśvatthāmā — Aśvatthāmā
      Droṇa's son — named after his cry at birth, which sounded like a horse's neigh (*aśva-sthāma*). One of the cursed immortals (cirañjīvī) of the tradition. His name on this list will eventually carry the night-massacre of the Pāṇḍava camp at the war's close — already inscribed here in verse 8.
    There are personalities like you, Bhīṣma, Karṇa, Kṛpa, Aśvatthāmā, Vikarṇa and the son of Somadatta called Bhūriśravā, who are always victorious in battle.
    Purport

    Duryodhana mentions the exceptional heroes in  the battle, all of whom are ever victorious. Vikarṇa is the brother of Duryodhana, Aśvatthāmā is the son of Droṇācārya, and Saumadatti, or Bhūriśravā, is the son of the King of the Bāhlīkas. Karṇa is the half brother of Arjuna, as he was born of Kuntī before her marriage with King Pāṇḍu. Kṛpācārya’s twin sister married Droṇācārya.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    8. There are yourself, Bhīṣma, Karṇa, Kṛpa, winner of wars, Aśvatthāmā, Vikarṇa, and Bhūriśravā. 9. There are also many other brave men who have given up their lives for my sake, skillful at fighting, armed with various missiles and weapons of close combat.
    Commentary

    Saumadatti refers to Bhūriśravā, the son of Somadatta.

    “They are willing to give up their lives in order to help me (tyakta-jīvitāḥ).” This is the intended meaning of Duryodhana, though the literal meaning is “They have given up their lives.” Actually however, Kṛṣṇa will later say: mayaivaite nihatāḥ pūrvam eva nimitta-mātraṁ bhava savyasācin These warriors have already been killed by Me before the war has started. You be My instrument, O Arjuna. BG 11.33 Thus, the literal meaning of Duryodhana’s words are thus completely true.

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    8-9. There are you, Bhīṣma, Karṇa, Kṛpa, troops of Droṇa and others which are winners of wars, Aśvatthāmā, Vikarṇa, Bhūriśravā, and Jayadratha. There are also many other brave men who have given up their lives for my sake, skillful at fighting, armed with various missiles and weapons of close combat.
    Commentary

    Bhavān refers to Droṇa. Vikarṇa was a younger brother of Duryodhana. Saumadatti refers to Bhūriśravā. The troops of Droṇa and others are described as victorious in war (samitiṁjayaḥ). “These are only the outstanding persons on my side. There are also other warriors whose numbers cannot be counted (anye ca). There are many (bahavaḥ) such as Jayadratha, Kṛtavarma and Śalya, who are determined to give up their lives for my sake if necessary (tyakta jīvitāḥ). “My victory will be accomplished because of their intense affection for me, their intense courage, and their knowledge of fighting.” This is his hint in speaking.

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    To encourage Dronacarya further, Duryodhana, mentions Krpa who is Dronacarya's brother‑in‑law (Drona is married with Krpi). And then Asvatthama, who is Drona's son. Duryodhana is very, very expert in presenting things in such a way to have his ends met. Vikarna is not in anyway as powerfull as the others, but he is the son of Dhrtarastra and he was the only one who protest against the offense to Draupadi in the assembly. Duryodhana is afraid that he may go over to the other side, so he mentions him amidst the great personalities.

    Personal Guidance
    There is value in respecting elders and tradition — but only when tradition is anchored to Kṛṣṇa, not to lineage alone.
    Practical Applications
    • Honor the elders in your life with one thoughtful gesture this week.
    • Distinguish between traditions that lead to Kṛṣṇa and traditions that merely flatter your ancestors.
    • Read or recall one teaching from Śrīla Prabhupāda's pranāma mantras to renew your reverence for paramparā.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where am I confusing inherited custom with eternal dharma?
    • Whom in my elder generation am I underutilizing as a spiritual resource?
    Analogy

    A list of names that begins with *your good self* and ends with Karṇa is a list designed for the listener's ego. Duryodhana names the elders first, the killers next, and his own line of loyalty is laid down by the order of recitation.

    Stories
    Bhīṣma at the head of Duryodhana's army

    Bhīṣma had vowed to defend the throne of Hastināpura whoever sat on it. When Duryodhana inherited that throne through political maneuvering, Bhīṣma's vow bound him to fight on the side his heart did not love. He told Yudhiṣṭhira privately on the eve of the war: "I am bound by my pledge, but my blessings are with you."

    Duryodhana names Bhīṣma here as a possession — listed between *bhavān* (your good self) and *karṇa* (Karṇa) — without seeming to feel the strangeness of the company. The great grandsire is reduced to a unit in a roster. The same Bhīṣma will, in seven verses, blow the *siṁha-nāda* conch and the inventory will become a man again.

    Important Words
    • śūrāḥ — heroes
      Same word he used for the *enemy* heroes in verse 4. Duryodhana applies *śūra* to both sides — a verbal admission of equality. The Gītā repeatedly forces the speaker to give the enemy the same nouns he gives himself.
    • mat - arthe — for my sake
      *Mat-* (mine) + *arthe* (for the sake of). The deepest pronoun of the chapter, the same possessive that opened it in verse 1 (*māmakāḥ*). Duryodhana's soldiers are *for him*. The Pāṇḍavas' soldiers, by contrast, will be told repeatedly that their actions are for Kṛṣṇa.
    • tyakta - jīvitāḥ — prepared to risk life
      Compound: *tyakta* (renounced) + *jīvita* (life). Literally "those by whom life has been given up." A rare moment of devotional language used in a mercenary cause — these men have *renounced their lives* for Duryodhana's project. The Gītā later asks what a *worthy* object of such renunciation looks like (the answer: Kṛṣṇa).
    • yuddha - viśāradāḥ — experienced in military science
      *Yuddha* (warfare) + *viśārada* (expert, accomplished). *Viśārada* is a high word — used elsewhere for masters of any difficult art. Duryodhana acknowledges his men are *experts*; but expertise alone, without dharma, will not save them. The chapter is quietly establishing that competence and morality come apart.
    There are many other heroes who are prepared to lay down their lives for my sake. All of them are well equipped with different kinds of weapons, and all are experienced in military science.
    Purport

    As far as the others are concerned – like Jayadratha, Kṛtavarmā and Śalya – all are determined to lay down their lives for Duryodhana’s sake. In other words, it is already concluded that all of them would die in the Battle of Kurukṣetra for joining the party of the sinful Duryodhana. Duryodhana was, of course, confident of his victory on account of the above-mentioned combined strength of his friends.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    8. There are yourself, Bhīṣma, Karṇa, Kṛpa, winner of wars, Aśvatthāmā, Vikarṇa, and Bhūriśravā. 9. There are also many other brave men who have given up their lives for my sake, skillful at fighting, armed with various missiles and weapons of close combat.
    Commentary

    Saumadatti refers to Bhūriśravā, the son of Somadatta.

    “They are willing to give up their lives in order to help me (tyakta-jīvitāḥ).” This is the intended meaning of Duryodhana, though the literal meaning is “They have given up their lives.” Actually however, Kṛṣṇa will later say: mayaivaite nihatāḥ pūrvam eva nimitta-mātraṁ bhava savyasācin These warriors have already been killed by Me before the war has started. You be My instrument, O Arjuna. BG 11.33 Thus, the literal meaning of Duryodhana’s words are thus completely true.

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    8-9. There are you, Bhīṣma, Karṇa, Kṛpa, troops of Droṇa and others which are winners of wars, Aśvatthāmā, Vikarṇa, Bhūriśravā, and Jayadratha. There are also many other brave men who have given up their lives for my sake, skillful at fighting, armed with various missiles and weapons of close combat.
    Commentary

    Bhavān refers to Droṇa. Vikarṇa was a younger brother of Duryodhana. Saumadatti refers to Bhūriśravā. The troops of Droṇa and others are described as victorious in war (samitiṁjayaḥ). “These are only the outstanding persons on my side. There are also other warriors whose numbers cannot be counted (anye ca). There are many (bahavaḥ) such as Jayadratha, Kṛtavarma and Śalya, who are determined to give up their lives for my sake if necessary (tyakta jīvitāḥ). “My victory will be accomplished because of their intense affection for me, their intense courage, and their knowledge of fighting.” This is his hint in speaking.

    Study Notes — Gauranga Priya Dāsa
    Gauranga Priya Dāsa Study
    Bhakti-śāstrī Notes, ISKCON Chowpatty (2009)
    Theme

    COMMON THEME: Duryodhana’s actions are described – They reveal his diplomacy and inner fear by the

    following indications:

    1. Duryodhana although mentioned as king, goes to the commander on account of seriousness of

    situation – quite fit to be a politician (1.2)

    2. Points out Drona’s mistake (of imparting military secrets to son of Drupada, Dhrstadyumna who was

    born to kill Dronacharya) to make him alert and uncompromising and warns that leniency would lead to

    defeat (1.3*)

    3. Mentions great heros equal to Bhima and Arjuna (1.4*)

    Why he compares them to Bhima and Arjuna –
    Because he knew the strength of Bhima and Arjuna
    Why he mentions other heros –
    Because they were great stumbling blocks on the path of victory as each and every one of them was as formidable and Bhima and Arjuna

    4. Mentions heros who are ready to lay down their lives for “me” (like Jayadratha, Krtavarma, Salya) (1.9)

    5. Praises Bhisma – He was confident of full support of Bhismadeva and Dronacarya because:

    They did not protect Draupadi when she was insulted
    Although Bhisma and Drona have affection for Pandavas and might become lenient, he hoped that they will give up all affection now (1.11)

    6. Asks for everyone’s support for Bhisma (1.11) – because

    Bhismadeva was undoubtedly the great hero, but he was an old man and the enemy might take advantage of his full engagement on one side
    He wanted everyone to feel important
    Focus of Learning

    PLEASE NOTE: Some points of these purports are covered under the main theme above

    (a) Why Sanjaya described Duryodhana’s actions first –

    Because Dhrtarashtra was blind from birth and also bereft of spiritual vision and he knew that his sons were equally blind in the matter of religion
    And Dhrtarashtra was afraid that under the influence of the place of pilgrimage, his sons may make some compromise

    (b) Study names of warriors on both sides (1.4 – 1.9)

    (c) Duryodhana compared Bhisma (more experienced general) to Bhima (less experienced general)

    (1.10*)

    Because Duryodhana knew if he should die at all he would be killed by Bhima and was therefore always envious of Bhima
    Bhima is like a fig in the presence of Bhisma

    (d) What made Duryodhana confident of victory (1.7 – 1.11)

    Above mentioned strength of his friends (1.7 – 1.9)
    Presence of Bhisma, a far superior General than Bhima – He clearly felt that victory of Kurus dependent on the presence of Bhismadeva (1.11)
    Confident of full support of Bhisma and Drona as they had shown during Draupadi’s insulting episode (1.11 purport)
    SUBSECTION B — SIGNS OF VICTORY OF PANDAVAS (1.12* — 1.20)

    COMMON THEME: Sanjaya tactfully informed Dhrtarashtra about “his hopeless plans to win” by giving the

    following indications and signs:

    SIGNS OF VICTORY OF PANDAVAS (9 points) 1. Krishna’s personal presence confirms victory
    Supreme Personality of Godhead is the charioteer (1.14) – “jayas tu pandu-putranam yesam…”
    Krishna as Hrsikesha directly controls the senses of a pure devotee

    2. Goddess of fortune

    Whenever and wherever the Lord is present, the goddess of fortune is also there
    She never lives without her husband; therefore all fortune is guaranteed (1.14)

    3. Venue

    Kurukshetra is a holy place (1.1)

    4. Hanumanji on Arjuna’s flag

    Hanumanji also helped Lord Rama in gaining victory (1.20)

    5. Symbol of Vishnu

    Conchshell is a symbol of Vishnu (1.12* & 1.14)
    This is indirectly indicated by Bhisma and Pandavas conchshells

    6. Transcendental conchshells

    Krishna and Arjuna’s conchshell mentioned as divya (transcendental) (1.14)

    7. Bhisma’s conchshell to pacify Duryodhana (1.12*)

    8. Agnideva’s Chariot given to Arjuna

    It was capable of conquering all directions (1.14)

    9. Shattering of hearts

    Conchshells of Pandavas shattered Kauravas hearts (1.19)
    Pandavas hearts not shattered – because of confidence in Krishna

    Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Classical
    Translation
    1.9 Sri Sankaracharya did not comment on this sloka. The commentary starts from 2.10.
    Śrī Rāmānujācārya Classical
    Translation
    1.1 - 1.19 Dhrtarastra said - Sanjaya said Duryodhana, after viewing the forces of Pandavas protected by Bhima, and his own forces protected by Bhisma conveyed his views thus to Drona, his teacher, about the adeacy of Bhima's forces for conering the Kaurava forces and the inadeacy of his own forces for victory against the Pandava forces. He was grief-stricken within. Observing his (Duryodhana's) despondecny, Bhisma, in order to cheer him, roared like a lion, and then blowing his conch, made his side sound their conchs and kettle-drums, which made an uproar as a sign of victory. Then, having heard that great tumult, Arjuna and Sri Krsna the Lord of all lords, who was acting as the charioteer of Arjuna, sitting in their great chariot which was powerful enough to coner the three worlds; blew their divine conchs Srimad Pancajanya and Devadatta. Then, both Yudhisthira and Bhima blew their respective conchs separately. That tumult rent asunder the hearts of your sons, led by Duryodhana. The sons of Dhrtarastra then thought, 'Our cause is almost lost now itself.' So said Sanjaya to Dhrtarastra who was longing for their victory. Sanjaya said to Dhrtarastra: Then, seeing the Kauravas, who were ready for battle, Arjuna, who had Hanuman, noted for his exploit of burning Lanka, as the emblem on his flag on his chariot, directed his charioteer Sri Krsna, the Supreme Lord-who is overcome by parental love for those who take shelter in Him who is the treasure-house of knowledge, power, lordship, energy, potency and splendour, whose sportive delight brings about the origin, sustentation and dissolution of the entire cosmos at His will, who is the Lord of the senses, who controls in all ways the senses inner and outer of all, superior and inferior - by saying, 'Station my chariot in an appropriate place in order that I may see exactly my enemies who are eager for battle.'

    Personal Guidance
    Many will offer to die for a cause out of pride or paycheck; Kṛṣṇa's devotees alone serve out of pure love.
    Practical Applications
    • Examine one loyalty you maintain — is it driven by pride, fear, devotion, or transaction?
    • Notice the difference between mercenary commitment and surrendered service in your work.
    • Offer one task today as service to Kṛṣṇa rather than as proof of your worth.
    Reflection Questions
    • What loyalties of mine are quietly transactional?
    • Where is my 'service' actually self-promotion in disguise?
    Analogy

    A king who says "there are *many other heroes* ready to die for me" without naming them is reaching for numbers because the names have run out. The unnamed *many* is the place where a confident inventory begins to slip into wishful thinking.

    Important Words
    • aparyāptam — immeasurable
      Ambiguous: *a-paryāpta* can mean *unlimited* (Duryodhana's intended sense) or *insufficient* (the slip of his tongue). Commentators have read it both ways. The very word he chooses for his own strength can mean *not enough*. The verse hands us his unconscious.
    • paryāptam — limited, sufficient
      The opposite-yet-twin of *aparyāpta*. Duryodhana means "the Pāṇḍava strength is limited." But *paryāpta* also means *adequate, complete*: their strength is *exactly enough*. Sanskrit allows the verse to mean both at once.
    • abhirakṣitam — perfectly protected
      *Abhi-rakṣ* — to *guard around*, to shield comprehensively. The word is used of *both* armies in this verse — Bhīṣma protects Duryodhana's side, Bhīma protects the Pāṇḍavas'. The vocabulary refuses to favour either side. The cosmos is impartial; the bias is the speaker's.
    • bhīṣma — by Grandfather Bhīṣma
      Repeated as the protective name of Duryodhana's army. But the Pāṇḍavas' protector — Bhīma — is the one named in the rhyming half of the verse. *Bhīṣma* and *Bhīma* both come from the root *bhī* (to be frightening). The two great fear-bearers are set side by side, and the verse hangs unresolved between them.
    Our strength is immeasurable, and we are perfectly protected by Grandfather Bhīṣma, whereas the strength of the Pāṇḍavas, carefully protected by Bhīma, is limited.
    Purport

    Herein an estimation of comparative strength is made by Duryodhana. He thinks that the strength of his armed forces is immeasurable, being specifically protected by the most experienced general, Grandfather Bhīṣma. On the other hand, the forces of the Pāṇḍavas are limited, being protected by a less experienced general, Bhīma, who is like a fig in the presence of Bhīṣma. Duryodhana was always envious of Bhīma because he knew perfectly well that if he should die at all, he would only be killed by Bhīma. But at the same time, he was confident of his victory on account of the presence of Bhīṣma, who was a far superior general. His conclusion that he would come out of the battle victorious was well ascertained.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    10. Our army protected by Bhīṣma is inadequate, but their army, protected by Bhīma is adequate.
    Commentary

    Our troops are not up to standard (aparyāptam): we cannot fight against the Pāṇḍavas. Even though protected all around by Bhīṣma, who has fine intelligence and is experienced in fighting and theory, Bhīṣma has sympathy for both parties. The Pāṇḍavas are very well protected (paryāptam abhirakṣitam) by Bhīma, though he has gross intelligence and is not thoroughly conversant with fighting and theory. In other words, they are well equipped to fight against us.

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    10. Our army protected by Bhīṣma is immeasurable, but their army, protected by Bhīma is limited.
    Commentary

    “But how can you achieve victory when the troops are equal on both sides?” “We have more troops. Our strength is immeasurable (aparyāptam) and is protected by Bhīṣma, who is most intelligent and an atiratha. The strength of the Pāṇḍavas’ army is limited (paryāptam), [Note: Rāmānuja takes the words aparyāptam to mean insufficient, and paryātam to mean sufficient. Viśvanātha and Śrīdhara follow the same interpretation. Madhuṣūdana Sarasvati takes the same meaning as Baladeva.] being protected Bhīma, who has very little intelligence and is only an ardha ratha. Thus I will attain victory.”

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Duryodhana has to make Bhisma feel very important. Bhisma's favorite students are the Pandavas. In this verse the word 'aparyaptam' has two different meanings. According to Srila Prabhupada and Srila Baladeva Vidyabhusana, it means 'immeasurable'. Because they are protected by Bhisma, their strength is immeasurable. When Bhisma hears that he becomes encouraged to fight stronger. But Viswanatha C. Thakura translates the word as 'insufficient', meaning that because Bhisma had great affection for the Pandavas, his being the protector of the Kauravas army, would be insufficient. That made Dronacarya feel important and very much needed to secure the victory for Duryodhana. Thus, by using this sublte word, Dronacarya could fire‑up, both great personalities. On the other side, Srila Madvacarya, didn't like the statement that the protection given by Bhima is limited. He was an incarnation of Vayu as Bhima.

    Study Notes — Gauranga Priya Dāsa
    Gauranga Priya Dāsa Study
    Bhakti-śāstrī Notes, ISKCON Chowpatty (2009)
    Theme

    COMMON THEME: Duryodhana’s actions are described – They reveal his diplomacy and inner fear by the

    following indications:

    1. Duryodhana although mentioned as king, goes to the commander on account of seriousness of

    situation – quite fit to be a politician (1.2)

    2. Points out Drona’s mistake (of imparting military secrets to son of Drupada, Dhrstadyumna who was

    born to kill Dronacharya) to make him alert and uncompromising and warns that leniency would lead to

    defeat (1.3*)

    3. Mentions great heros equal to Bhima and Arjuna (1.4*)

    Why he compares them to Bhima and Arjuna –
    Because he knew the strength of Bhima and Arjuna
    Why he mentions other heros –
    Because they were great stumbling blocks on the path of victory as each and every one of them was as formidable and Bhima and Arjuna

    4. Mentions heros who are ready to lay down their lives for “me” (like Jayadratha, Krtavarma, Salya) (1.9)

    5. Praises Bhisma – He was confident of full support of Bhismadeva and Dronacarya because:

    They did not protect Draupadi when she was insulted
    Although Bhisma and Drona have affection for Pandavas and might become lenient, he hoped that they will give up all affection now (1.11)

    6. Asks for everyone’s support for Bhisma (1.11) – because

    Bhismadeva was undoubtedly the great hero, but he was an old man and the enemy might take advantage of his full engagement on one side
    He wanted everyone to feel important
    Focus of Learning

    PLEASE NOTE: Some points of these purports are covered under the main theme above

    (a) Why Sanjaya described Duryodhana’s actions first –

    Because Dhrtarashtra was blind from birth and also bereft of spiritual vision and he knew that his sons were equally blind in the matter of religion
    And Dhrtarashtra was afraid that under the influence of the place of pilgrimage, his sons may make some compromise

    (b) Study names of warriors on both sides (1.4 – 1.9)

    (c) Duryodhana compared Bhisma (more experienced general) to Bhima (less experienced general)

    (1.10*)

    Because Duryodhana knew if he should die at all he would be killed by Bhima and was therefore always envious of Bhima
    Bhima is like a fig in the presence of Bhisma

    (d) What made Duryodhana confident of victory (1.7 – 1.11)

    Above mentioned strength of his friends (1.7 – 1.9)
    Presence of Bhisma, a far superior General than Bhima – He clearly felt that victory of Kurus dependent on the presence of Bhismadeva (1.11)
    Confident of full support of Bhisma and Drona as they had shown during Draupadi’s insulting episode (1.11 purport)
    SUBSECTION B — SIGNS OF VICTORY OF PANDAVAS (1.12* — 1.20)

    COMMON THEME: Sanjaya tactfully informed Dhrtarashtra about “his hopeless plans to win” by giving the

    following indications and signs:

    SIGNS OF VICTORY OF PANDAVAS (9 points) 1. Krishna’s personal presence confirms victory
    Supreme Personality of Godhead is the charioteer (1.14) – “jayas tu pandu-putranam yesam…”
    Krishna as Hrsikesha directly controls the senses of a pure devotee

    2. Goddess of fortune

    Whenever and wherever the Lord is present, the goddess of fortune is also there
    She never lives without her husband; therefore all fortune is guaranteed (1.14)

    3. Venue

    Kurukshetra is a holy place (1.1)

    4. Hanumanji on Arjuna’s flag

    Hanumanji also helped Lord Rama in gaining victory (1.20)

    5. Symbol of Vishnu

    Conchshell is a symbol of Vishnu (1.12* & 1.14)
    This is indirectly indicated by Bhisma and Pandavas conchshells

    6. Transcendental conchshells

    Krishna and Arjuna’s conchshell mentioned as divya (transcendental) (1.14)

    7. Bhisma’s conchshell to pacify Duryodhana (1.12*)

    8. Agnideva’s Chariot given to Arjuna

    It was capable of conquering all directions (1.14)

    9. Shattering of hearts

    Conchshells of Pandavas shattered Kauravas hearts (1.19)
    Pandavas hearts not shattered – because of confidence in Krishna
    Classical Ācāryas
    Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Classical
    Translation
    1.10 Sri Sankaracharya did not comment on this sloka. The commentary starts from 2.10.
    Śrī Rāmānujācārya Classical
    Translation
    1.1 - 1.19 Dhrtarastra said - Sanjaya said Duryodhana, after viewing the forces of Pandavas protected by Bhima, and his own forces protected by Bhisma conveyed his views thus to Drona, his teacher, about the adeacy of Bhima's forces for conering the Kaurava forces and the inadeacy of his own forces for victory against the Pandava forces. He was grief-stricken within. Observing his (Duryodhana's) despondecny, Bhisma, in order to cheer him, roared like a lion, and then blowing his conch, made his side sound their conchs and kettle-drums, which made an uproar as a sign of victory. Then, having heard that great tumult, Arjuna and Sri Krsna the Lord of all lords, who was acting as the charioteer of Arjuna, sitting in their great chariot which was powerful enough to coner the three worlds; blew their divine conchs Srimad Pancajanya and Devadatta. Then, both Yudhisthira and Bhima blew their respective conchs separately. That tumult rent asunder the hearts of your sons, led by Duryodhana. The sons of Dhrtarastra then thought, 'Our cause is almost lost now itself.' So said Sanjaya to Dhrtarastra who was longing for their victory. Sanjaya said to Dhrtarastra: Then, seeing the Kauravas, who were ready for battle, Arjuna, who had Hanuman, noted for his exploit of burning Lanka, as the emblem on his flag on his chariot, directed his charioteer Sri Krsna, the Supreme Lord-who is overcome by parental love for those who take shelter in Him who is the treasure-house of knowledge, power, lordship, energy, potency and splendour, whose sportive delight brings about the origin, sustentation and dissolution of the entire cosmos at His will, who is the Lord of the senses, who controls in all ways the senses inner and outer of all, superior and inferior - by saying, 'Station my chariot in an appropriate place in order that I may see exactly my enemies who are eager for battle.'
    Śrī Abhinavagupta Classical
    Translation
    1.10 Aparyaptam etc. For us, for Pandava army grauded by Bhimasena is unlimited, i.e., it is not possible to vanish; or it is not sufficient, i.e., very insignificant when compared with our army. This is the meaning. On the other hand, for these Pandavas, this army guarded by Bhisma, belonging to us, is limited i.e., it is possible to vanish; or it is sufficient i.e., too much; in other words it is not possible to be vanished in the war by these (Pandavas).
    Swami Sivananda Classical
    Translation
    1.10. "This army of ours marshalled by Bhishma is insufficient, whereas that army of theirs marshelled by Bhima is sufficient.
    Commentary

    1.10 अपर्याप्तम् insufficient? तत् that? अस्माकम् ours? बलम् army? भीष्माभिरक्षितम् marshalled by Bhishma? पर्याप्तम् sufficient? तु while? इदम् this? एतेषाम् their? बलम् army? भीमाभिरक्षितम् marshalled by Bhima.Commentary The verse is differently interpreted by different commentators. Sridhara Swami takes the word aparyaptam to mean insufficient. Ananda Giri takes it to mean unlimited.

    Swami Gambhīrānanda Classical
    Translation
    1.10 Therefore, our army under the complete protection of Bhisma and others is unlimited. But this army of these (enemies), under the protection of Bhima and others is limited.
    Shri Purohit Swami Classical
    Translation
    1.10 Yet our army seems the weaker, though commanded by Bheeshma; their army seems the stronger, though commanded by Bheema.

    Personal Guidance
    Numerical strength dazzles materialists; spiritual strength comes from one soul with Kṛṣṇa on his side.
    Practical Applications
    • Stop estimating spiritual progress by external metrics (followers, influence, attendance).
    • Recall one moment when small sincere effort yielded great spiritual fruit.
    • Replace 'how many' with 'how sincere' in your reflections this week.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where am I impressed by quantity when I should be evaluating quality?
    • How is Kṛṣṇa already on my side in ways I have not noticed?
    Analogy

    Saying "our strength is immeasurable" while in the next breath admitting that the other side's strength is "limited" but well-protected is the language of a man trying to convince himself. Duryodhana is the ocean boasting to the river that he is *larger* — but a fixed lake of fresh water can do what no ocean can.

    Important Words
    • ayaneṣu — in the strategic points
      *Ayana* — a passage, an avenue, a *way*. The same root we meet in *Rāmāyaṇa* ("Rāma's way") and *uttarāyaṇa* (the sun's northward course). Duryodhana speaks of the army's *ways* — every avenue must funnel support to Bhīṣma. The Gītā will reuse this very word for *paths of yoga*.
    • yathā - bhāgam — as differently arranged
      *Yathā* (according to) + *bhāga* (portion, share). Each warrior has his *bhāga*, his allotment. The Gītā later applies this same logic to dharma — each soul has its own *svabhāga* of duty, not transferable to another.
    • abhirakṣantu — should give support, protect
      Same root *abhi-rakṣ* as verse 10. Imperative plural — *let all of you protect Bhīṣma*. Duryodhana asks the protectors to protect the protector. The recursion shows the brittleness of the structure: when one node carries all the weight, every other node exists only to defend that one node.
    All of you must now give full support to Grandfather Bhīṣma, as you stand at your respective strategic points of entrance into the phalanx of the army.
    Purport

    Duryodhana, after praising the prowess of Bhīṣma, further considered that others might think that they had been considered less important, so in his usual diplomatic way, he tried to adjust the situation in the above words. He emphasized that Bhīṣmadeva was undoubtedly the greatest hero, but he was an old man, so everyone must especially think of his protection from all sides. He might become engaged in the fight, and the enemy might take advantage of his full engagement on one side. Therefore, it was important that other heroes not leave their strategic positions and allow the enemy to break the phalanx. Duryodhana clearly felt that the victory of the Kurus depended on the presence of Bhīṣmadeva. He was confident of the full support of Bhīṣmadeva and Droṇācārya in the battle because he well knew that they did not even speak a word when Arjuna’s wife Draupadī, in her helpless condition, had appealed to them for justice while she was being forced to appear naked in the presence of all the great generals in the assembly. Although he knew that the two generals had some sort of affection for the Pāṇḍavas, he hoped that these generals would now completely give it up, as they had done during the gambling performances.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    11. Situated in your positions for attack, you should protect Bhīṣma on all sides.
    Commentary

    Therefore you should be very careful. Though you are divided into different groups (yathā-bhāgam) for the purpose of entering into the enemy lines (ayaneṣu), you should not give up your designated positions on the battlefield. Being fixed in your respective positions, protect Bhīṣma on all sides, so that he will not be attacked from behind while engaged in fighting with others. The implication here is “Only by the strength of Bhīṣma will we survive.”

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    11. Situated in your positions for entering the enemy flanks, you should all protect Bhīṣma on all sides.
    Commentary

    “If Droṇa understands the meaning of my words, he may become indifferent to fighting himself. This will damage my plans. Therefore I will give him personal responsibility in this war.” Thus he spoke. “You should protect Bhīṣma on all sides by staying in your positions which have been designated individually for entering into the ranks of the enemy troops (āyaneṣu). Act in this way so that he will not be attacked by others, since being absorbed in fighting, he will not be looking on the sides or behind. My victory will be accomplished while Bhīṣma, the general, is unaware of my arrangements.” The intention is as follows. Bhīṣma is our grandfather. You are our teacher. You two I know to be my fervent well-wishers, for though you knew the injustice I did at the gambling match you did not speak a word when Draupadī asked for justice.” He thus made his request so that Droṇa would give up his trace of affection for the Pāṇḍavas that was still visible.

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Duryodhana here indicates very clearly that the victory depends very much on the presence of Bhisma. And also as an expert diplomat he is showing that the support of the all army is very, very important.

Then, having heard that great tumult, Arjuna and Sri Krsna the Lord of all lords, who was acting as the charioteer of Arjuna, sitting in their great chariot which was powerful enough to coner the three worlds; blew their divine conchs Srimad Pancajanya and Devadatta. Then, both Yudhisthira and Bhima blew their respective conchs separately. That tumult rent asunder the hearts of your sons, led by Duryodhana. The sons of Dhrtarastra then thought, 'Our cause is almost lost now itself.' So said Sanjaya to Dhrtarastra who was longing for their victory. Sanjaya said to Dhrtarastra: Then, seeing the Kauravas, who were ready for battle, Arjuna, who had Hanuman, noted for his exploit of burning Lanka, as the emblem on his flag on his chariot, directed his charioteer Sri Krsna, the Supreme Lord-who is overcome by parental love for those who take shelter in Him who is the treasure-house of knowledge, power, lordship, energy, potency and splendour, whose sportive delight brings about the origin, sustentation and dissolution of the entire cosmos at His will, who is the Lord of the senses, who controls in all ways the senses inner and outer of all, superior and inferior - by saying, 'Station my chariot in an appropriate place in order that I may see exactly my enemies who are eager for battle.'

    Personal Guidance
    Strategic reliance on a single great pillar can be wisdom — or it can be evasion of personal responsibility.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice where you outsource spiritual responsibility to one person (guru, teacher, leader) in unhealthy ways.
    • Take up one practice this week that you cannot delegate — your daily japa, your honesty with yourself.
    • Express genuine gratitude to the senior devotees who hold your community together.
    Reflection Questions
    • Whom am I leaning on heavily — and is that leaning surrender, or avoidance?
    • What spiritual responsibility have I quietly handed off that I should reclaim?
    Analogy

    An army that pins its survival on one grandfather's strategic point is like a fleet that has tied every ship to a single anchor. The anchor may hold for a day. But when the wind turns, all ships go down together.

    Stories
    Śikhaṇḍī, the appointed bow

    Bhīṣma was unbreakable so long as no one stood opposite him whom he would refuse to fight. The Pāṇḍavas remembered that, decades earlier, Bhīṣma had vowed never to lift a weapon against a woman — and that Śikhaṇḍī, though now a man, had been born female. On the tenth day of the war, Arjuna shot from behind Śikhaṇḍī's chariot, and the grandsire fell on a bed of arrows.

    Duryodhana, in this verse, has staked everything on Bhīṣma. The very next chapters of the war will show that putting all your support on one pillar — however vast — is not strategy but evasion. Real defence is distributed; pinning your dharma on one man's vow leaves you ten days from collapse.

    Important Words
    • kuru - vṛddhaḥ — the eldest of the Kurus
      *Vṛddha* — old, grown, increased. The same root as *Vṛddha-Garga*, *vṛddhi*. Bhīṣma is the *vṛddha* — the elder by years and by dharmic seniority. The Gītā at every step honours the principle: the *vṛddha* speaks first.
    • pitāmahaḥ — the grandfather
      *Pitā* (father) + *maha* (great). Vyāsa keeps stacking Bhīṣma's honorifics: in one verse he is *kuru-vṛddha*, *pitāmaha*, *pratāpa-vān*. Three titles for one man, because the conch is being blown not by a soldier but by an institution.
    • siṁha - nādam — lion's roar
      *Siṁha* (lion) + *nāda* (sound). A specific kṣatriya sound — the lion-cry. Same image used elsewhere for great kings and ascetics alike. Bhīṣma is the *Kuru-siṁha*; the conch makes his voice audible across the field.
    • śaṅkham — conchshell
      *Śaṅkha* — the conch is the standard Vaiṣṇava emblem (Viṣṇu holds one in his upper-left hand). Vyāsa is quietly transferring the iconography: even the Kaurava grandsire's signal is, in essence, a Vaiṣṇava instrument. The Lord's symbols cannot be monopolized by His ostensible side.
    • pratāpa - vān — the valiant
      *Pratāpa* — fierce splendour, the heat of a king's authority. *-vān* — possessing. Same root *tap* (to heat, to burn) as *tapas*. Bhīṣma's valour is a *tapas*. His celibate vow is itself an inner fire, and the conch is the outward flame from that long-banked heat.
    Then Bhīṣma, the great valiant grandsire of the Kuru dynasty, the grandfather of the fighters, blew his conchshell very loudly, making a sound like the roar of a lion, giving Duryodhana joy.
    Purport

    The grandsire of the Kuru dynasty could understand the inner meaning of the heart of his grandson Duryodhana, and out of his natural compassion for him he tried to cheer him by blowing his conchshell very loudly, befitting his position as a lion. Indirectly, by the symbolism of the conchshell, he informed his depressed grandson Duryodhana that he had no chance of victory in the battle, because the Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa was on the other side. But still, it was his duty to conduct the fight, and no pains would be spared in that connection.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    12. Then the majestic elder among the Kurus, the grandfather, in order to bring joy to Duryodhana, making the sound of lion, blew his conch loudly.
    Commentary

    Bhīṣma, the elder of the Kurus, joyful on hearing respect given to him, and to produce joy in Duryodhana by driving away his fears, roaring like lion, blew his conch shell. The phrase siṁha-nādaṁ vinadya uses the same root nad twice. The literal meaning is “roaring the roar of a lion.” The intended meaning is “roaring like a lion,” according to the sūtra upamāne karmaṇi. (Aṣṭādhyāyī, Pāṇini 3.4.45)

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    12. Then the majestic elder among the Kurus, the grandfather, in order to bring joy to Duryodhana, making the sound of lion, blew his conch loudly.
    Commentary

    Then Bhīṣma in great joy, understanding that Duryodhana was praising him, blew his conch shell to drive away the inner fear of Duryodhana. The use of the phrase siṁha nādam vinadya is according to the Pāṇini rule upamāne karmaṇi ca. (Pāṇini 3.4.45) Ca refers to another sūtra to denote an agent as well as an object: kartary upamāne. (Pāṇini 3.2.79) It means “sounding like a lion.” [Note: A verb root with the suffix “am” can be used to mean “like.” Thus siṁha-nadam vinadya means that he blew his conch, sounding like a lion. Another example would be aja-nāśam nastaḥ: he perished like a goat (perishes).] Without saying a word, just by blowing his conch, Bhīṣma announced that he would give up his life according to kṣatriya dharma for Duryodhana, though victory or defeat was really dependent only on the Lord.

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Duryodhana shows his expertise in firing‑up Bhisma, and Bhisma is responding by blowing the conchshell and get ready for the fight. Here is shown one of the various symbolisms that indicate the side of the victorious ‑ the conchshell blown by Bhisma. It indicates indirectly that the sons of Dhrtarastra have no chance of victory, because the conchshell is the symbol of Visnu or Krsna. Bhisma would do his best but the victory was not garanteed at all.

    Study Notes — Gauranga Priya Dāsa

    Personal Guidance
    A senior devotee's clear voice — like Bhīṣma's conch — re-anchors a bewildered community in dharma.
    Practical Applications
    • Listen carefully when a senior Vaiṣṇava speaks; their words often carry more weight than their volume suggests.
    • When you feel scattered, return to Prabhupāda's recorded voice or letters for re-orientation.
    • Be the steady voice in your home or community when others are anxious.
    Reflection Questions
    • Whose 'conch' do I rally to when I am bewildered?
    • Where am I called to be that steadying voice for someone else?
    Analogy

    An old lion's roar from the cliff at dusk does not threaten the prey — it cheers the cubs of his own pride. Bhīṣma's conch is no battle-cry first; it is grandfather's reassurance to a worried grandson.

    Stories
    Bhīṣma's lifelong vow

    When his father Śāntanu loved the fisherwoman Satyavatī but could not marry her because of his prince's claim, the young Devavrata vowed before all to renounce the throne and to live celibate forever — so that Satyavatī's sons could inherit unchallenged. The gods, watching, called him *Bhīṣma*: "the man of the terrible vow."

    For decades, this vow has held the Kuru house together — through the deaths of his half-brothers, the regency over his blind nephew, the rise of his great-nephews. Now, on the brink of the war he has tried to prevent, the old grandsire blows his conch like a lion's roar — *siṁha-nādam* — to cheer his despondent grandson Duryodhana. Behind the lion-sound is a sad love. The man who held the family together is now signalling its destruction. He blows the conch anyway, because his vow gave him no other place to stand.

    Important Words
    • śaṅkhāḥ — conchshells
      Plural now — many conches answer the one. The verse expands from Bhīṣma's solitary *siṁha-nāda* (v.12) to a chorus. Each conch is a small Vaiṣṇu-symbol in a kṣatriya hand. Vyāsa is layering Vaiṣṇava iconography even on the unrighteous side.
    • bheryaḥ — large drums
      *Bherī* — the war-drum, used in Vedic processions and royal anointments. The drum names the formal status of the assembly: this is not a brawl but a sacrificial event. The Kurukṣetra war was understood by both sides as a *yajña* — a sacrifice of warriors.
    • paṇava - ānaka — small drums and kettledrums
      *Paṇava* (small two-headed drum) + *ānaka* (kettledrum). The full instrumentation of a royal procession. Vyāsa lists them precisely because the war is being staged with full Vedic protocol — no detail of ritual is being skipped, however much dharma is being violated.
    • tumulaḥ — tumultuous
      Same root underlying English *tumult*. The compound sound is so dense it cannot be parsed into separate instruments — it has become a single roaring mass. The chapter is building, sonically, toward Arjuna's collapse: the louder the sound, the heavier the silence after it (v.46).
    After that, the conchshells, drums, bugles, trumpets and horns were all suddenly sounded, and the combined sound was tumultuous.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    13. Then conches, kettle drums, small drums, and larger drums were suddenly sounded, making a tumultuous roar.
    Commentary

    Both sides became eager to fight. This is described in this verse. Paṇava is a type of drum. Ānaka is a kettle drum. Gomukha is a type of trumpet.

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    13. Then conches, kettle drums, small drums, and larger drums were suddenly sounded, making a tumultuous roar.
    Commentary

    When Bhīṣma blew his conch, at that time, in his army, suddenly instruments and conches began to sound. Abhyahanyanta is a reflexive passive, literally meaning “the instruments were sounded by themselves” or “the instruments made sounds.” Paṇava, ānaka, and gomukha are types of instruments. The sound was very great since the instruments sounded all at once.

    

    Focus of Learning

    (a) Sanjaya very tactfully informed King Dhrtarashtra of the following points through all the above

    mentioned verses:

    His unwise policy of deceiving the sons of Pandu and endeavoring to enthrone his own sons was not very laudable
    All the signs indicate that the whole Kuru dynasty would be killed
    From the grandsire Bhisma to the grandson Abhimanyu, and all the kings of all states were doomed
    And Dhrtarashtra was the cause of the whole catastrophe because he encouraged the policy followed by his sons

    (a) Message announced by conchshells – Blowing of conchshells announced the message that

    Kauravas were predestined to lose the battle

    (b) Importance of names

    Hrsikesha
    Owner of all senses / senses of living entities are part and parcels of His senses

    ▪ Impersonalists cannot account for the senses of the living entities and they are

    always anxious to describe the living entities as sense-less or impersonal

    Lord as Paramatma directs the senses according to the surrender of the living entity
    Directly controls transcendental senses of a pure devotee like Arjuna
    Govinda – Pleasure-giver to cows and senses
    Dhananjaya – Arjuna helped elder brother to fetch wealth for different sacrifices
    Vrkodara – Eat as voraciously as he could do herculean tasks (Bhima)
    Few other names explained – Madhusudana / Vasudeva / Devaki-nandana / Yasoda-nandana / Partha-sarthy (Read 1.15 purport)

    Translation
    1.13 Sri Sankaracharya did not comment on this sloka. The commentary starts from 2.10.
    Śrī Rāmānujācārya Classical
    Translation
    1.1 - 1.19 Dhrtarastra said - Sanjaya said Duryodhana, after viewing the forces of Pandavas protected by Bhima, and his own forces protected by Bhisma conveyed his views thus to Drona, his teacher, about the adeacy of Bhima's forces for conering the Kaurava forces and the inadeacy of his own forces for victory against the Pandava forces. He was grief-stricken within. Observing his (Duryodhana's) despondecny, Bhisma, in order to cheer him, roared like a lion, and then blowing his conch, made his side sound their conchs and kettle-drums, which made an uproar as a sign of victory. Then, having heard that great tumult, Arjuna and Sri Krsna the Lord of all lords, who was acting as the charioteer of Arjuna, sitting in their great chariot which was powerful enough to coner the three worlds; blew their divine conchs Srimad Pancajanya and Devadatta. Then, both Yudhisthira and Bhima blew their respective conchs separately. That tumult rent asunder the hearts of your sons, led by Duryodhana. The sons of Dhrtarastra then thought, 'Our cause is almost lost now itself.' So said Sanjaya to Dhrtarastra who was longing for their victory. Sanjaya said to Dhrtarastra: Then, seeing the Kauravas, who were ready for battle, Arjuna, who had Hanuman, noted for his exploit of burning Lanka, as the emblem on his flag on his chariot, directed his charioteer Sri Krsna, the Supreme Lord-who is overcome by parental love for those who take shelter in Him who is the treasure-house of knowledge, power, lordship, energy, potency and splendour, whose sportive delight brings about the origin, sustentation and dissolution of the entire cosmos at His will, who is the Lord of the senses, who controls in all ways the senses inner and outer of all, superior and inferior - by saying, 'Station my chariot in an appropriate place in order that I may see exactly my enemies who are eager for battle.'

    Personal Guidance
    When dharma sounds, the whole field responds — the cosmos reverberates with the announcement of righteous action.
    Practical Applications
    • Begin gatherings with the chanting of Kṛṣṇa's names — let the sound vibration set the field.
    • Notice how a single sincere chant in the morning shifts the texture of your whole day.
    • Be willing to be the one who breaks the silence with Hare Kṛṣṇa when no one else will.
    Reflection Questions
    • What sound vibrations dominate my mornings — devotional or distracting?
    • Am I willing to be the first conch in a room full of hesitation?
    Analogy

    When one conch is answered by every conch, drum, and horn of an army, it is no longer a signal — it is a single body proving it can still move. The thunder is less an announcement than a self-test. Duryodhana's side answers Bhīṣma with sound because silence after the grandsire's roar would have been unbearable.

    Important Words
    • śvetaiḥ — with white
      Vedic colour-coding: *śveta* = pure, sāttvika, brāhmaṇa-like. Arjuna's chariot is yoked to the colour of sattva. Krishna's chariot driving is the yoking of action (kṣatriya) to purity (brāhmaṇa) — the very synthesis the Gītā will later teach.
    • syandane — in a chariot
      *Syandana* — from *syand* (to flow, to run swiftly). The chariot is the *flowing one*, the moving platform. The Upaniṣads use the chariot as the body-image (Kaṭha 1.3.3: *ātmānaṁ rathinaṁ viddhi*). Vyāsa here puts the Lord *as charioteer* on a chariot — anticipating the metaphor that lets the whole Gītā be heard as Kṛṣṇa driving the soul.
    • mādhavaḥ — Kṛṣṇa, husband of the goddess of fortune
      *Mā* (Lakṣmī) + *dhava* (husband). The first of Kṛṣṇa's many names in the Gītā — and it is His relational name, not His personal one. Vyāsa introduces Him as *Lakṣmī's lord*. Fortune itself rides on this chariot.
    • pāṇḍavaḥ — Arjuna, son of Pāṇḍu
      Arjuna is named only as *Pāṇḍu's son* — by lineage, not by personal name. Vyāsa pairs *Mādhava* with *Pāṇḍava* — Lakṣmī's lord beside Pāṇḍu's son. The two relational names sit in dignified balance: Lord and devotee, named not by ego but by belonging.
    • divyau — transcendental
      *Divya* — from *div* (to shine, the heavens). Same root as *deva*, *divine*. The opposing conches were earthly *śaṅkhāḥ*; these are *divyau śaṅkhau*. Two conches, dual number — the Lord and His servant always sound together. The Gītā's whole theology of *nāma-saṅkīrtana* is foreshadowed here: divine sound, sounded in pairs.
    On the other side, both Lord Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, stationed on a great chariot drawn by white horses, sounded their transcendental conchshells.
    Purport

    In contrast with the conchshell blown by Bhīṣmadeva, the conchshells in the hands of Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna are described as transcendental. The sounding of the transcendental conchshells indicated that there was no hope of victory for the other side because Kṛṣṇa was on the side of the Pāṇḍavas. Jayas tu pāṇḍu-putrāṇāṁ yeṣāṁ pakṣe janārdanaḥ. Victory is always with persons like the sons of Pāṇḍu because Lord Kṛṣṇa is associated with them. And whenever and wherever the Lord is present, the goddess of fortune is also there because the goddess of fortune never lives alone without her husband. Therefore, victory and fortune were awaiting Arjuna, as indicated by the transcendental sound produced by the conchshell of Viṣṇu, or Lord Kṛṣṇa. Besides that, the chariot on which both the friends were seated had been donated by Agni (the fire-god) to Arjuna, and this indicated that this chariot was capable of conquering all sides, wherever it was drawn over the three worlds.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    14. Then Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, standing in a large chariot yoked with white horses, blew their divine conches.
    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    14. Then Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, standing in a large chariot yoked with white horses, blew their divine conches.
    Commentary

    In this verse, the desire to fight which arose in the troops of the Pāṇḍavas is described. Though the others were also standing in their chariots, Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna are particularly mentioned in this regard to indicate the special nature of the chariot, which was given by Agni himself, [Note: The chariot, quiver, horses were given to Arjuna and cakra to Kṛṣṇa by Agni before he devoured the Khāṇḍava forest.] which had great power and could conquer the three worlds.

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Here are a few more symbols indicating the Pandavas' victory: Krsna is on their side. Krsna and Arjuna's conchshells are called 'divyau',transcendental. Where Krsna is present there is also Laksmidevi, the goddess of fortune.

    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa and the pure devotee blow their conches together — the Lord and His servant always work in unison.
    Practical Applications
    • When you serve, picture yourself working alongside a great devotee, not alone.
    • Read about Arjuna's friendship with Kṛṣṇa to feel the sweetness of confidential service.
    • Allow Kṛṣṇa to act through you today — set aside the burden of being the doer.
    Reflection Questions
    • When I serve, am I aware of Kṛṣṇa as my companion, or only as my employer?
    • What 'conch' has Kṛṣṇa given me to blow — and am I sounding it?
    Analogy

    When the Lord and His friend stand on one chariot drawn by white horses and blow their conches together, the sound is not louder than the enemy's — it is *different*. A single transcendental note set against a hundred war-drums: small in volume, infinite in source.

    Stories
    The white horses of Arjuna's chariot

    Arjuna's chariot was given by Agni, the fire-god, after Arjuna helped him consume the Khāṇḍava forest. Its four white horses came from the celestial regions, gifted by Citraratha the king of the Gandharvas. The chariot was indestructible and the banner was Hanumān himself, who had agreed to ride along until the war's end.

    Now Kṛṣṇa drives this chariot. Vyāsa names the colour of the horses — *śveta* — because whiteness in Vedic poetry is the colour of purity, of brāhmaṇa-knowledge, of Sarasvatī. The Lord and the kṣatriya ride together, drawn by purity itself, and from this chariot the *divyau śaṅkhau* — transcendental conches — are sounded. The opposing side blew earthly conches; this side blows *divine* ones. The verse already hints at the unequal sources of sound.

    Important Words
    • pāñcajanyam — the conchshell named Pāñcajanya
      From the demon Pañcajana. The Lord's primary conch is a converted enemy — a doctrinal hint that surrender transforms the asura into an instrument of the Lord's voice. (See Bhāgavatam 10.45.)
    • hṛṣīka - īśaḥ — Hṛṣīkeśa, lord of the senses
      *Hṛṣīka* (the senses) + *īśa* (lord). One of Kṛṣṇa's most theologically loaded names — He is the *master of the senses*. The Gītā's whole teaching on *sense-control* is sealed in this epithet: only the One who owns the senses can teach how to discipline them.
    • devadattam — the conchshell named Devadatta
      *Deva* (god) + *datta* (given). Arjuna's conch was given by the gods. The contrast with the opposing side: their conches are theirs by purchase or inheritance; the devotee's conch is *deva-datta* — gifted from above. Even the instrument of service is grace.
    • dhanam - jayaḥ — Arjuna, winner of wealth
      *Dhanam* (wealth) + *jaya* (conqueror). Arjuna's epithet from the Rājasūya conquests — he gathered tribute from all the kings of Bhārata for Yudhiṣṭhira's sacrifice. The Gītā uses many epithets for Arjuna; each names a quality Kṛṣṇa is about to ask him to *redirect inward*. The winner of outer wealth must now win inner wealth.
    • bhīma - karmā — one who performs herculean tasks
      *Bhīma* (fearsome) + *karmā* (deeds). Bhīma's epithet — he of fearsome deeds. The same root as *bhīṣma* (terrible) and *bhayam* (fear). On the field face the same fear-root: *bhīṣma* the grandsire, *bhīma* the grandson-by-blood. Vyāsa is collecting the fear-words on both sides.
    Lord Kṛṣṇa blew His conchshell, called Pāñcajanya; Arjuna blew his, the Devadatta; and Bhīma, the voracious eater and performer of herculean tasks, blew his terrific conchshell, called Pauṇḍra.
    Purport

    Lord Kṛṣṇa is referred to as Hṛṣīkeśa in this verse because He is the owner of all senses. The living entities are part and parcel of Him, and therefore the senses of the living entities are also part and parcel of His senses. The impersonalists cannot account for the senses of the living entities, and therefore they are always anxious to describe all living entities as senseless, or impersonal. The Lord, situated in the hearts of all living entities, directs their senses. But He directs in terms of the surrender of the living entity, and in the case of a pure devotee He directly controls the senses. Here on the Battlefield of Kurukṣetra the Lord directly controls the transcendental senses of Arjuna, and thus His particular name of Hṛṣīkeśa. The Lord has different names according to His different activities. For example, His name is Madhusūdana because He killed the demon of the name Madhu; His name is Govinda because He gives pleasure to the cows and to the senses; His name is Vāsudeva because He appeared as the son of Vasudeva; His name is Devakī-nandana because He accepted Devakī as His mother; His name is Yaśodā-nandana because He awarded His childhood pastimes to Yaśodā at Vṛndāvana; His name is Pārtha-sārathi because He worked as charioteer of His friend Arjuna. Similarly, His name is Hṛṣīkeśa because He gave direction to Arjuna on the Battlefield of Kurukṣetra. Arjuna is referred to as Dhanañjaya in this verse because he helped his elder brother in fetching wealth when it was required by the king to make expenditures for different sacrifices. Similarly, Bhīma is known as Vṛkodara because he could eat as voraciously as he could perform herculean tasks, such as killing the demon Hiḍimba. So the particular types of conchshell blown by the different personalities on the side of the Pāṇḍavas, beginning with the Lord’s, were all very encouraging to the fighting soldiers. On the other side there were no such credits, nor the presence of Lord Kṛṣṇa, the supreme director, nor that of the goddess of fortune. So they were predestined to lose the battle – and that was the message announced by the sounds of the conchshells.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    15-16. Kṛṣṇa blew Pāṣcajanya, Arjuna blew Devadatta, and Bhīma of fearful deeds blew the great conch Pauṇḍra. Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, blew Anantavijaya, and Nakula and Sahadeva blew their conches Sughoṣa and Manipuṣpaka. 17-18. Then the king of Kāśī, the greatest archer, Śikhaṇḍī, a mahā-ratha, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Virāṭa and Sātyaki, who could not be defeated, Drupada, the sons of Draupadī, and mighty-armed Abhimanyu blew their conches one after the other.
    Commentary

    The names of the conch shells are listed here, starting with Kṛṣṇa’s Pāṣcajanya.

    The word aparājitaḥ means unconquerable. However, it can be read cāpa rājitaḥ, by including the previous ca as part of the word instead a separate word meaning “and”, in which case it means “equipped with a bow.”

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    15-16. Kṛṣṇa blew Paṣcajanya, Arjuna blew Devadatta, and Bhīma of fearful deeds blew the great conch Pauṇḍra. Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, blew Anantavijaya, and Nakula and Sahadeva blew their conches Sughoṣa and Manipuṣpaka. 17-18. Then the king of Kāṣī, who was the greatest archer, the mahāratha Śikhaṇḍi, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Virāṭa and Sātyaki, who shone with his bow, Drupada, the sons of Draupadī, and mighty-armed Ahimanyu blew their conches one after the other, O lord of the earth.
    Commentary

    The names of the conches starting with Kṛṣṇa’s Paṅcajanya are listed. The word hṛṣikeśa (master of the senses) used in describing the Lord indicates that the Lord would help this army (He would help by directing their senses skilfully). Mentioning the names of the conches indicates that these persons had many conches of divine nature. The word rājā indicates that Yudhiṣṭhira had performed the rājāsūya sacrifice. [Note: He was not recognized as king until after the battle.] The word bhīma karma (man of ferocious actions) indicates that Bhīma had killed many demons such as Hiḍimbā. The word dhanaṣjaya indicates that Arjuna had gathered unlimited treasures when he went out to conquer the directions. Thus the outstanding nature of the Pāṇḍava army is indicated. The opposing army, not having these descriptive names, was therefore inferior. Kāśya indicates the king of Kāśi, who was a great archer (parameṣvāsaḥ). Sātyaki was shining with his bow (cāpa rājitaḥ). “O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of the earth (pṛthivī pate), your bad advice has brought about this calamity in the form of the destruction of the dynasty.” That is the suggestion of addressing the king as “lord of the earth.”

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Lord Krsna blew His conchshell, called Pancajanya; Arjuna blew his, the Devadatta; and Bhima, the voracious eater and performer of herculean tasks, blew his terrific conchshell, called Paundra. (cn/DS) Here the name used for Krsna is 'Hrsikesa' which means 'the Lord directs the senses of the living entities'. This is a very significant name for Krsna, which also indicates His victory because one only succeeds in anything by the use of the senses. Krsna was sitting there as the 'controller of the senses'. And when the devotee surrenders to Krsna, He personaly directs his senses. Arjuna was not there on his own prowess. Srila Prabhupada says in his Purport: "Lord Krsna is referred to as Hrsikesa in this verse because He is the owner of all senses. The living entities are part and parcel of Him, and therefore the senses of the living entities are also part and parcel of His senses. The impersonalists cannot account for the senses of the living entities, and therefore they are always anxious to describe all living entities as sense‑less, or impersonal. The Lord, situated in the hearts of all living entities, directs their senses. But He directs in terms of the surrender of the living entity, and in the case of a pure devotee He directly controls the senses. Here on the Battlefield of Kuruksetra the Lord directly controls the transcendental senses of Arjuna, and thus His particular name of Hrsikesa. The Lord has different names according to His different activities. For example, His name is Madhusudana because He killed the demon of the name Madhu; His name is Govinda because He gives pleasure to the cows and to the senses; His name is Vasudeva because He appeared as the son of Vasudeva; His name is Devaki‑nandana because He accepted Devaki as His mother; His na Yasoda‑nandana because He awarded His childhood pastimes to Yasoda at Vrndavana; His name is Partha‑sarathi because He worked as charioteer of His friend Arjuna. Similarly, His name is Hrsikesa because He gave direction to Arjuna on the Battlefield of Kuruksetra. Arjuna is referred to as Dhananjaya in this verse because he helped his elder brother in fetching wealth when it was re quired by the king to make expenditures for different sacrifices. Similarly, Bhima is known as Vrkodara because he could eat as voraciously as he could perform herculean tasks, such as killing the demon Hidimba. So the particular types of conchshell blown by the different personalities on the side of the Pandavas, beginning with the Lord's, were all encouraging to the fighting soldiers. On the other side there were no such credits, nor the presence of Lord Krsna, the supreme director, nor that of the goddess of fortune. So they were predestined to lose the battle‑‑and that was the message announced by the sounds of the conchshells." The sound of the conchshells announced the defeat of Dhrtarastra's sons since so many signs of victory were on the side of the Pandavas.
