    Pandavas’ above. Purports for Texts 1.15 to 1.18 are presented in the ‘Focus of Learning’ sections below

    

    Focus of Learning

    (a) Sanjaya very tactfully informed King Dhrtarashtra of the following points through all the above

    mentioned verses:

    His unwise policy of deceiving the sons of Pandu and endeavoring to enthrone his own sons was not very laudable
    All the signs indicate that the whole Kuru dynasty would be killed
    From the grandsire Bhisma to the grandson Abhimanyu, and all the kings of all states were doomed
    And Dhrtarashtra was the cause of the whole catastrophe because he encouraged the policy followed by his sons

    (a) Message announced by conchshells – Blowing of conchshells announced the message that

    Kauravas were predestined to lose the battle

    (b) Importance of names

    Hrsikesha
    Owner of all senses / senses of living entities are part and parcels of His senses

    ▪ Impersonalists cannot account for the senses of the living entities and they are

    always anxious to describe the living entities as sense-less or impersonal

    Lord as Paramatma directs the senses according to the surrender of the living entity
    Directly controls transcendental senses of a pure devotee like Arjuna
    Govinda – Pleasure-giver to cows and senses
    Dhananjaya – Arjuna helped elder brother to fetch wealth for different sacrifices
    Vrkodara – Eat as voraciously as he could do herculean tasks (Bhima)
    Few other names explained – Madhusudana / Vasudeva / Devaki-nandana / Yasoda-nandana / Partha-sarthy (Read 1.15 purport)
    Classical Ācāryas
    Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Classical
    Translation
    1.15 Sri Sankaracharya did not comment on this sloka. The commentary starts from 2.10.
    Śrī Rāmānujācārya Classical
    Translation
    1.1 - 1.19 Dhrtarastra said - Sanjaya said Duryodhana, after viewing the forces of Pandavas protected by Bhima, and his own forces protected by Bhisma conveyed his views thus to Drona, his teacher, about the adeacy of Bhima's forces for conering the Kaurava forces and the inadeacy of his own forces for victory against the Pandava forces. He was grief-stricken within. Observing his (Duryodhana's) despondecny, Bhisma, in order to cheer him, roared like a lion, and then blowing his conch, made his side sound their conchs and kettle-drums, which made an uproar as a sign of victory. Then, having heard that great tumult, Arjuna and Sri Krsna the Lord of all lords, who was acting as the charioteer of Arjuna, sitting in their great chariot which was powerful enough to coner the three worlds; blew their divine conchs Srimad Pancajanya and Devadatta. Then, both Yudhisthira and Bhima blew their respective conchs separately. That tumult rent asunder the hearts of your sons, led by Duryodhana. The sons of Dhrtarastra then thought, 'Our cause is almost lost now itself.' So said Sanjaya to Dhrtarastra who was longing for their victory. Sanjaya said to Dhrtarastra: Then, seeing the Kauravas, who were ready for battle, Arjuna, who had Hanuman, noted for his exploit of burning Lanka, as the emblem on his flag on his chariot, directed his charioteer Sri Krsna, the Supreme Lord-who is overcome by parental love for those who take shelter in Him who is the treasure-house of knowledge, power, lordship, energy, potency and splendour, whose sportive delight brings about the origin, sustentation and dissolution of the entire cosmos at His will, who is the Lord of the senses, who controls in all ways the senses inner and outer of all, superior and inferior - by saying, 'Station my chariot in an appropriate place in order that I may see exactly my enemies who are eager for battle.'

    Personal Guidance
    Each devotee blows a uniquely-named conch; your service has a specific shape no one else can replicate.
    Practical Applications
    • Stop comparing your sādhana to that of others — your conch sounds in your voice, not theirs.
    • Identify your own particular service offering and commit to it more deeply.
    • Honor the diversity of Vaiṣṇava expression in your community.
    Reflection Questions
    • What is the unique shape of the service I am called to render?
    • Where am I diluting my offering by trying to sound like someone else?
    Analogy

    Each conch on this chariot bears a personal name — Pāñcajanya, Devadatta, Pauṇḍra. The Lord does not blow an anonymous shell. Service has a name; devotion is named; the divine recognizes each instrument that is offered.

    Stories
    Pāñcajanya, the demon-conch

    The conch Kṛṣṇa blows is Pāñcajanya — taken from the body of the demon Pañcajana, whom Kṛṣṇa slew in the depths of the sea when rescuing the dead son of His guru Sāndīpani. The demon had taken the form of a great conch-shell; Kṛṣṇa pulled him out of the ocean and used his shell ever after. (Bhāgavatam 10.45.40–48.)

    So the very conch the Lord now sounds on the field of Kurukṣetra was earlier the body of a demon — transformed into the Lord's instrument through being defeated. There is a quiet doctrine here: what was once an obstacle, once it has surrendered, becomes the medium through which the Lord announces dharma.

    📝 My note

    Important Words
    • ananta - vijayam — the conch named Ananta-vijaya
      *Ananta* (endless) + *vijaya* (victory). Yudhiṣṭhira, who has known mostly defeat, blows the conch of *endless victory*. The name foreshadows the Gītā's redefinition of *jaya*: not outer triumph but inner constancy.
    • sughoṣa - maṇipuṣpakau — the conches Sughoṣa and Maṇipuṣpaka
      *Su-ghoṣa* ("sweet-sounding") and *Maṇi-puṣpaka* ("jewel-flowered"). Nakula and Sahadeva, the youngest twins, blow conches whose very names are aesthetic — sweet sound and jewel-flowering. Beauty has its place in dharma's chorus.
    • mahā - rathaḥ — one who can fight ten thousand bowmen
      The kṣatriya rating reappears — now applied to Śikhaṇḍī, the appointed instrument of Bhīṣma's fall. Vyāsa positions the future grandsire-slayer in a list of *mahā-rathas* without comment; the chapter has begun threading the war's outcome into its opening cast-list.
    • aparājitaḥ — the unconquered
      *A-parājita* — never defeated. Sātyaki's epithet. The verse positions an *unconquered* warrior on the Pāṇḍava side — a quiet rebuttal of Duryodhana's verses 4–9, where he listed strong enemies but could call none *aparājita*.
    • pṛthak pṛthak — each separately
      Repetition of *pṛthak* — *separately, separately*. Each warrior's conch is sounded *individually*. Vyāsa is making a point: the Pāṇḍava chorus is not undifferentiated noise; each devotee's voice is distinct. The collective is built of named individuals.
    King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, blew his conchshell, the Ananta-vijaya, and Nakula and Sahadeva blew the Sughoṣa and Maṇipuṣpaka. That great archer the King of Kāśī, the great fighter Śikhaṇḍī, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Virāṭa, the unconquerable Sātyaki, Drupada, the sons of Draupadī, and others, O King, such as the mighty-armed son of Subhadrā, all blew their respective conchshells.
    Purport

    Sañjaya informed King Dhṛtarāṣṭra very tactfully that his unwise policy of deceiving the sons of Pāṇḍu and endeavoring to enthrone his own sons on the seat of the kingdom was not very laudable. The signs already clearly indicated that the whole Kuru dynasty would be killed in that great battle. Beginning with the grandsire, Bhīṣma, down to the grandsons like Abhimanyu and others – including kings from many states of the world – all were present there, and all were doomed. The whole catastrophe was due to King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, because he encouraged the policy followed by his sons.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    15-16. Kṛṣṇa blew Pāṣcajanya, Arjuna blew Devadatta, and Bhīma of fearful deeds blew the great conch Pauṇḍra. Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, blew Anantavijaya, and Nakula and Sahadeva blew their conches Sughoṣa and Manipuṣpaka. 17-18. Then the king of Kāśī, the greatest archer, Śikhaṇḍī, a mahā-ratha, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Virāṭa and Sātyaki, who could not be defeated, Drupada, the sons of Draupadī, and mighty-armed Abhimanyu blew their conches one after the other.
    Commentary

    The names of the conch shells are listed here, starting with Kṛṣṇa’s Pāṣcajanya.

    The word aparājitaḥ means unconquerable. However, it can be read cāpa rājitaḥ, by including the previous ca as part of the word instead a separate word meaning “and”, in which case it means “equipped with a bow.”

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    15-16. Kṛṣṇa blew Paṣcajanya, Arjuna blew Devadatta, and Bhīma of fearful deeds blew the great conch Pauṇḍra. Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, blew Anantavijaya, and Nakula and Sahadeva blew their conches Sughoṣa and Manipuṣpaka. 17-18. Then the king of Kāṣī, who was the greatest archer, the mahāratha Śikhaṇḍi, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Virāṭa and Sātyaki, who shone with his bow, Drupada, the sons of Draupadī, and mighty-armed Ahimanyu blew their conches one after the other, O lord of the earth.
    Commentary

    The names of the conches starting with Kṛṣṇa’s Paṅcajanya are listed. The word hṛṣikeśa (master of the senses) used in describing the Lord indicates that the Lord would help this army (He would help by directing their senses skilfully). Mentioning the names of the conches indicates that these persons had many conches of divine nature. The word rājā indicates that Yudhiṣṭhira had performed the rājāsūya sacrifice. [Note: He was not recognized as king until after the battle.] The word bhīma karma (man of ferocious actions) indicates that Bhīma had killed many demons such as Hiḍimbā. The word dhanaṣjaya indicates that Arjuna had gathered unlimited treasures when he went out to conquer the directions. Thus the outstanding nature of the Pāṇḍava army is indicated. The opposing army, not having these descriptive names, was therefore inferior. Kāśya indicates the king of Kāśi, who was a great archer (parameṣvāsaḥ). Sātyaki was shining with his bow (cāpa rājitaḥ). “O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of the earth (pṛthivī pate), your bad advice has brought about this calamity in the form of the destruction of the dynasty.” That is the suggestion of addressing the king as “lord of the earth.”

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    King Yudhisthira, the son of Kunti, blew his conchshell, the Ananta‑vijaya, and Nakula and Sahadeva blew the Sughosa and Manipuspaka. That great archer the King of Kasi, the great fighter Sikhandi, Dhrstadyumna, Virata, the unconquerable Satyaki, Drupada, the sons of Draupadi, and the others, O King, such as the mighty‑armed son of Subhadra, all blew their respective conchshells. (cn/DS) All these conchshells had very significant importance. Only all these warriors whose conchshells had names, survived the battlefield. Except the unconquerable Satyaki who also survived.

    

    Focus of Learning

    (a) Sanjaya very tactfully informed King Dhrtarashtra of the following points through all the above

    mentioned verses:

    His unwise policy of deceiving the sons of Pandu and endeavoring to enthrone his own sons was not very laudable
    All the signs indicate that the whole Kuru dynasty would be killed
    From the grandsire Bhisma to the grandson Abhimanyu, and all the kings of all states were doomed
    And Dhrtarashtra was the cause of the whole catastrophe because he encouraged the policy followed by his sons

    (a) Message announced by conchshells – Blowing of conchshells announced the message that

    Kauravas were predestined to lose the battle

    (b) Importance of names

    Hrsikesha
    Owner of all senses / senses of living entities are part and parcels of His senses

    ▪ Impersonalists cannot account for the senses of the living entities and they are

    always anxious to describe the living entities as sense-less or impersonal

    Lord as Paramatma directs the senses according to the surrender of the living entity
    Directly controls transcendental senses of a pure devotee like Arjuna
    Govinda – Pleasure-giver to cows and senses
    Dhananjaya – Arjuna helped elder brother to fetch wealth for different sacrifices
    Vrkodara – Eat as voraciously as he could do herculean tasks (Bhima)
    Few other names explained – Madhusudana / Vasudeva / Devaki-nandana / Yasoda-nandana / Partha-sarthy (Read 1.15 purport)

    Śrī Rāmānujācārya Classical
    Translation
    1.1 - 1.19 Dhrtarastra said - Sanjaya said Duryodhana, after viewing the forces of Pandavas protected by Bhima, and his own forces protected by Bhisma conveyed his views thus to Drona, his teacher, about the adeacy of Bhima's forces for conering the Kaurava forces and the inadeacy of his own forces for victory against the Pandava forces. He was grief-stricken within. Observing his (Duryodhana's) despondecny, Bhisma, in order to cheer him, roared like a lion, and then blowing his conch, made his side sound their conchs and kettle-drums, which made an uproar as a sign of victory. Then, having heard that great tumult, Arjuna and Sri Krsna the Lord of all lords, who was acting as the charioteer of Arjuna, sitting in their great chariot which was powerful enough to coner the three worlds; blew their divine conchs Srimad Pancajanya and Devadatta. Then, both Yudhisthira and Bhima blew their respective conchs separately. That tumult rent asunder the hearts of your sons, led by Duryodhana. The sons of Dhrtarastra then thought, 'Our cause is almost lost now itself.' So said Sanjaya to Dhrtarastra who was longing for their victory. Sanjaya said to Dhrtarastra: Then, seeing the Kauravas, who were ready for battle, Arjuna, who had Hanuman, noted for his exploit of burning Lanka, as the emblem on his flag on his chariot, directed his charioteer Sri Krsna, the Supreme Lord-who is overcome by parental love for those who take shelter in Him who is the treasure-house of knowledge, power, lordship, energy, potency and splendour, whose sportive delight brings about the origin, sustentation and dissolution of the entire cosmos at His will, who is the Lord of the senses, who controls in all ways the senses inner and outer of all, superior and inferior - by saying, 'Station my chariot in an appropriate place in order that I may see exactly my enemies who are eager for battle.'

    Personal Guidance
    Many devotees, named together, sound dharma in concert — collective service amplifies what individual service alone cannot achieve.
    Practical Applications
    • Participate in a kīrtana you would normally skip; experience the multiplication of effect in collective chanting.
    • Show up for a community service even when your particular skill is not the headline contribution.
    • Trust that even minor participation matters when the whole community is sounding dharma.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where do I disqualify myself from collective service because my role feels small?
    • How does my voice become richer when joined with others'?
    Analogy

    Many conches, each separately named — *pṛthak pṛthak* — sound across the field. This is not a single voice but a chorus of distinct devotional notes. Each devotee has his own conch, his own sound. The Lord's army is recognizable by individuality, not uniformity.

    Stories
    Yudhiṣṭhira and Ananta-vijaya

    Yudhiṣṭhira's conch is named *Ananta-vijaya* — "infinite victory." It is a strange name for a king whose lifetime has been one long defeat — exiled twice, dressed in bark, his wife humiliated, his brothers separated, his kingdom gambled away. He has not been a winner in any worldly arithmetic.

    Yet the conch knows what the world does not. *Ananta-vijaya* — the *endless* victory — is the victory that survives every loss because it is not located in outcomes. Kṛṣṇa will later teach Arjuna exactly this in chapter 2: that the inner victory of steady dharma cannot be undone by outer defeat. The eldest Pāṇḍava blows the conch that names the Gītā's own thesis.

    Important Words
    • ghoṣaḥ — vibration
      *Ghoṣa* — sound, but specifically the *vibratory continuation* of a sound, the hum that lingers. Same root as in *Su-ghoṣa* (Nakula's conch in v.16). The verse moves from named conches to a single resonant *ghoṣa* — many sources, one effect.
    • hṛdayāni — hearts
      *Hṛdaya* — the seat of feeling and of the *ātman* in the Upaniṣads. The plural is significant: not one heart but *all* the hearts of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons are simultaneously cracked. Sound that goes for the heart is the Vedic measure of true mantra.
    • vyadārayat — shattered
      Causative imperfect of *dṝ* (to tear, to split). Same root as *dāraṇa*. The verb is violent: the conch-sound *tore* the Kaurava hearts. Sound, in the Vedic worldview, is not metaphor — it is physical work done on the inner organ.
    • tumulaḥ — uproarious
      Same word that described the Kaurava drumming in v.13. Vyāsa repeats it precisely. The two sides produce *tumult*; only one side's tumult *shatters hearts*. Mere noise does not equal sacred vibration. The same volume can be empty or transformative depending on its source.
    • abhyanunādayan — resounding
      *Abhi-anu-nad* — to resound, to echo through. The Vedic image of a mantra that *fills the field*. Kurukṣetra is being saturated with the sound of dharma before the first arrow flies. The war has been won, sonically, before it begins.
    The blowing of these different conchshells became uproarious. Vibrating both in the sky and on the earth, it shattered the hearts of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
    Purport

    When Bhīṣma and the others on the side of Duryodhana blew their respective conchshells, there was no heart-breaking on the part of the Pāṇḍavas. Such occurrences are not mentioned, but in this particular verse it is mentioned that the hearts of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra were shattered by the sounds vibrated by the Pāṇḍavas’ party. This is due to the Pāṇḍavas and their confidence in Lord Kṛṣṇa. One who takes shelter of the Supreme Lord has nothing to fear, even in the midst of the greatest calamity.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda

The sound of the conches of the followers of Dhṛtarāṣṭra did not cause any agitation in the hearts of the Pāṇdāvas, because nothing was mentioned of this.

    1.1 - 1.19 Dhrtarastra said - Sanjaya said Duryodhana, after viewing the forces of Pandavas protected by Bhima, and his own forces protected by Bhisma conveyed his views thus to Drona, his teacher, about the adeacy of Bhima's forces for conering the Kaurava forces and the inadeacy of his own forces for victory against the Pandava forces. He was grief-stricken within. Observing his (Duryodhana's) despondecny, Bhisma, in order to cheer him, roared like a lion, and then blowing his conch, made his side sound their conchs and kettle-drums, which made an uproar as a sign of victory. Then, having heard that great tumult, Arjuna and Sri Krsna the Lord of all lords, who was acting as the charioteer of Arjuna, sitting in their great chariot which was powerful enough to coner the three worlds; blew their divine conchs Srimad Pancajanya and Devadatta. Then, both Yudhisthira and Bhima blew their respective conchs separately. That tumult rent asunder the hearts of your sons, led by Duryodhana. The sons of Dhrtarastra then thought, 'Our cause is almost lost now itself.' So said Sanjaya to Dhrtarastra who was longing for their victory. Sanjaya said to Dhrtarastra: Then, seeing the Kauravas, who were ready for battle, Arjuna, who had Hanuman, noted for his exploit of burning Lanka, as the emblem on his flag on his chariot, directed his charioteer Sri Krsna, the Supreme Lord-who is overcome by parental love for those who take shelter in Him who is the treasure-house of knowledge, power, lordship, energy, potency and splendour, whose sportive delight brings about the origin, sustentation and dissolution of the entire cosmos at His will, who is the Lord of the senses, who controls in all ways the senses inner and outer of all, superior and inferior - by saying, 'Station my chariot in an appropriate place in order that I may see exactly my enemies who are eager for battle.'

    Personal Guidance
    When dharma sounds with unified voice, even hardened opposition feels its tremor — sincere devotion carries authority by itself.
    Practical Applications
    • Trust that sincere chanting and service makes its impact felt without your needing to argue.
    • Stop trying to convince adversaries through debate; let your steady devotional life speak.
    • Notice the moments when even a closed heart momentarily softens at the sound of Hare Kṛṣṇa.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where am I exhausting myself in argument when sincere practice would be the louder testimony?
    • Whose hardened heart might be more affected by my steadiness than by my words?
    Analogy

    When the sound of dharma resounds, it does not break stone walls — it shatters hearts. The Pāṇḍava conches reach the Kauravas not through the ear but through the chest. A heart full of unrighteous purpose cannot bear the vibration of a righteous note.

    O King .
    Important Words
    • kapi - dhvajaḥ — he whose flag was marked with Hanumān
      *Kapi* (monkey) + *dhvaja* (flag-pole, banner). Hanumān himself rides on Arjuna's banner — a literal continuation of Rāmāyaṇa-Vaiṣṇavism into the Mahābhārata. Where the Lord descends, His perfect servant remains close. The flag is no symbol; it is the servant in residence.
    • pravṛtte — while about to engage
      Locative absolute of *pra-vṛt* — to set in motion, to begin. The same root as *pravṛtti* (engagement in action), which the Gītā will later contrast with *nivṛtti* (withdrawal). The verb names the very turning-point the Gītā addresses: the moment of *being about to act*.
    • dhanuḥ — bow
      The kṣatriya emblem. Same word as in the Upaniṣadic image of the *praṇava-dhanuḥ* ("OM is the bow," Muṇḍaka 2.2.4). Arjuna's bow is also a metaphor: lifted, in this verse; dropped, in verse 47; lifted again only after the Gītā has taught him what to aim at.
    • udyamya — taking up
      Absolutive of *ud-yam* — to lift up, to raise. The same root as *udyama* (effort, exertion). Arjuna's first movement of the Gītā is *udyama* — exertion. The whole text is a question about how *udyama* should be directed.
    • hṛṣīkeśam — unto Lord Kṛṣṇa
      Accusative of *Hṛṣīkeśa* — the Lord of the senses. Arjuna addresses Kṛṣṇa, in his first speech, as *lord of the senses*. Before he says anything else, the soul has acknowledged the right hierarchy: the senses' lord is being asked to drive the chariot of the senses' agent.
    At that time Arjuna, the son of Pāṇḍu, seated in the chariot bearing the flag marked with Hanumān, took up his bow and prepared to shoot his arrows. O King, after looking at the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra drawn in military array, Arjuna then spoke to Lord Kṛṣṇa these words.
    Purport

    The battle was just about to begin. It is understood from the above statement that the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra were more or less disheartened by the unexpected arrangement of military force by the Pāṇḍavas, who were guided by the direct instructions of Lord Kṛṣṇa on the battlefield. The emblem of Hanumān on the flag of Arjuna is another sign of victory because Hanumān cooperated with Lord Rāma in the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa, and Lord Rāma emerged victorious. Now both Rāma and Hanumān were present on the chariot of Arjuna to help him. Lord Kṛṣṇa is Rāma Himself, and wherever Lord Rāma is, His eternal servitor Hanumān and His eternal consort Sītā, the goddess of fortune, are present. Therefore, Arjuna had no cause to fear any enemies whatsoever. And above all, the Lord of the senses, Lord Kṛṣṇa, was personally present to give him direction. Thus, all good counsel was available to Arjuna in the matter of executing the battle. In such auspicious conditions, arranged by the Lord for His eternal devotee, lay the signs of assured victory.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    20-23. O King, then, as the armies prepared to fight, Arjuna with Hanumān’s insignia on his flag, seeing the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra standing there, taking his bow in hand, spoke to Hṛṣīkeśa: O Acyuta please station my chariot between the two armies, so I can view at the commencement of the war those situated with a desire to fight, and those with whom I should fight. I see that those who have gathered here, desiring to please the foolish sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, are intent on fighting.
    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    20-23. O King, then, as the armies prepared to fight, Arjuna with Hanuman insignia on his flag, seeing the sons of Dhṛtrāṣṭra standing there, taking his bow in hand, spoke to Hṛṣīkeśa: O Acyuta, please station my chariot between the two armies, so I can view at the commencement of the war those standing desirous of fighting, and those with whom I should fight. I believe that those who have gathered here, desiring to please the foolish sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, are intent on fighting.
    Commentary

    Mahīpate means “O Dhṛtarāstra.” Arjuna then spoke. “O Acyuta, you do not deviate from your innate nature—from your affection for your devotee, or from your supreme power. Controlled by this quality, without fear, place my chariot according my words, the words of your devotee.” He then speaks of the purpose of doing so. ‘Place the chariot so that I can see who are situated firmly, not trembling in fear (avasthitān), who are desirous of fighting (yoddu kamān), with no desire for compromise.” “But you are fighter, not a spectator. What will be accomplished by viewing this?” “I wish to see at the beginning of the battle those friends and relatives in whose company I will fight, and those friends and relatives against whom I will fight. For that purpose, place my chariot between the two armies. ” “Out of friendship they will make peace.” “No, there will be no conciliation between the two sides. I believe (avekṣe) that they are intent on fighting (yotsyamānām). They are intent on fighting, desiring to please the son of Dhṛtarāstra who is unintelligent (durbuddheḥ), ignorant of means for his own survival (ignorant that he is going to die), even in face of this war, which does not sober his intelligence. Therefore my viewing the rival party in war has been justified. ”

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya

O King, after looking at the sons of Dhrtarastra drawn in military array, Arjuna then spoke to Lord Krsna these words. (cn/DS) The same points are mentioned again, indicating the Pandavas' victory: ‑ The name Hrsikesa for Krsna, ‑ Hanuman is in the flag of Arjuna's chariot, ‑ Krsna also means Rama ‑ where is Rama, there is Sita, the goddess of fortune. ‑ "And above all, the Lord of the senses, Lord Krsna, was personally present to give him (Arjuna) direction. Thus, all good counsel was available to Arjuna in the matter of executing the battle. In such auspicious conditions, arranged by the Lord for His eternal devotee, lay the signs of assured victory."
    Study Notes — Gauranga Priya Dāsa
    Gauranga Priya Dāsa Study
    Bhakti-śāstrī Notes, ISKCON Chowpatty (2009)
    Theme

    The atmosphere was surcharged. The world’s most powerful kṣatriyas had gathered to fight and

    were filled with the spirit of battle. This war differed from the situation Śrīla Prabhupāda criticized in

    the 1960s, when the United States drafted students, not kṣatriyas, and forced them into battle.

    These men were fighting men. Fighting was in their blood. Just as devotees come to Vṛndāvana or

    Māyāpur from all around the world, these kṣatriyas came from all over the world to fight. They had

    faith that dying on the battlefield would gain them entrance into the heavenly planets.

    Bhagavad Gita Notes

    The two armies were in formation. Conchshells blew. The hair of warriors stood on end in anticipa-

    tion. Kṛṣṇa was with Arjuna on his chariot.

    Hanumān, decorating the chariot’s flag, was ready to shout his war cries to help Bhīma terrify the

    enemy. Earlier, the Mahābhārata had described a meeting between Hanumān and Bhīma. Once,

    while Arjuna was seeking celestial weapons, the remaining Pāṇḥavas wandered to Badarikāśrama,

    high in the Himālayas. Suddenly, the Ālakananda River carried to Draupadī a beautiful and fragrant

    thousand-petaled lotus flower. Draupadī was captivated by its beauty and scent. “Bhīma, this lotus

    flower is so beautiful. I should offer it to Yudhiṣṭhira Mahārāja. Could you get me a few more? We

    could take some back to our hermitage in Kāmyaka.”

    Bhīma grabbed his club and charged up the hill where no mortals were permitted. As he ran, he

    bellowed and frightened elephants and lions. He uprooted trees as he pushed them aside. Not car-

    ing for the ferocious beasts of the jungle, he climbed a steep mountain until his progress was

    blocked by a huge monkey lying across the path.

    “Why are you making so much noise and scaring all the animals?” the monkey said. “Just sit down

    and eat some fruit.”

    “Move aside,” ordered Bhīma, for etiquette forbade him to step over the monkey. The monkey’s

    reply?

    “I am too old to move. Jump over me.”

    Bhīma, becoming angry, repeated his order, but the monkey, again pleading the weakness of old

    age, requested Bhīma to simply move his tail aside. Unlimitedly powerful Bhīma grabbed the tail and

    tried, but failed. Amazed, he respectfully inquired as to the monkey’s identity and was overjoyed to

    learn that he had met his brother Hanumān, for both Bhīma and Hanumān were sons of Vāyu. Ha-

    numān first embraced Bhīma and showed him the huge form in which he had leaped to Laìkā. He

    then offered Bhīma the following blessings.

    “I shall remain present on the flag of your brother Arjuna. When you roar like a lion on the battle-

    field, my voice will join with yours to strike terror into the hearts of your enemies. You will be victo-

    rious and regain your kingdom.”

    Now Arjuna, his chariot driven by Kṛṣṇa and marked with the flag of Hanumān, picked up his bow.

    The horses and elephants moved excitedly. The opening arrows of the long-awaited battle were

    now to be released. Arjuna, just on the brink of battle, spoke the following words.

    Personal Guidance
    Arjuna takes up his bow at the moment of dharma — be ready to act when the moment of duty arrives.
    Practical Applications
    • Identify one duty you have been avoiding; commit to acting on it within the week.
    • Stop waiting for perfect circumstances — Kṛṣṇa wants you to begin from where you stand.
    • Pick up your tools (japa beads, books, service materials) the moment the call sounds.
    Reflection Questions
    • What duty have I been quietly postponing?
    • What 'bow' have I left unstrung that Kṛṣṇa is asking me to take up?
    Analogy

    Arjuna lifts his bow not yet to shoot, but to inquire. The *bow being raised* is the body's question. The mind cannot yet ask what the hands are already asking: *show me what I am about to do*.

    Stories
    Hanumān on the flag

    When Arjuna was returning from his pilgrimage with Subhadrā, he passed through Rāmeśvaram. There he met Hanumān — the eternal servant of Rāma — who, hearing of the coming war, agreed to ride on Arjuna's banner until the war ended. The *kapi-dhvaja* — "the flag bearing the monkey" — is therefore not decoration but a literal presence: Hanumān himself riding above Arjuna's chariot.

    So on this chariot Kṛṣṇa holds the reins, Hanumān rides the flagstaff, and Arjuna sits between them. The same chariot was earlier set on fire by Aśvatthāmā's astras — and only after the war's end, when Kṛṣṇa stepped down and Hanumān flew away, did the wood collapse into ash. The chariot held because of who rode on it, not because of itself. Arjuna's lifting of the bow takes place inside this guarded geometry.

    Important Words
    • madhye — between
      Locative of *madhya* — middle, midst. The Gītā's geographical setting in a single word: the chariot is placed *in the middle* between the two armies. The teaching happens *between* contending forces, not on either side. The dharmic vantage is always *between*, never *with*.
    • sthāpaya — please keep, station
      Imperative of causative *sthā* — *cause to stand*. Arjuna's first command to Kṛṣṇa is to *station* the chariot. Sanskrit dharma-discourse uses *sthā* obsessively (*sthita-prajña*, *sthiti*, *avasthāna*). To be *placed* is the first condition; what one does next depends on where one stands.
    • acyuta — O infallible one
      *A-cyuta* — never fallen. From *cyu* (to fall). Kṛṣṇa is *the one who never falls*. Arjuna addresses Him by this epithet precisely as he himself is about to fall. The infallible one is asked to station the falling one.
    • nirīkṣe — may look upon
      First-person optative of *ni-īkṣ* — to look attentively, to examine. *Nirīkṣe aham* — "let *me* see." The Gītā's opening movement is the soul asking for *sight*, not for victory. Direct examination of one's situation is the first step of dharmic action.
    • yoddhu - kāmān — desiring to fight
      Same desiderative root *yudh* as *yuyutsavaḥ* in v.1. The chapter began with Dhṛtarāṣṭra naming those *desiring to fight*; Arjuna ends his request with the same desiderative. The two men, blind father and seeing warrior, ask about the same desire. One asks from anxiety; one asks from dharma.
    Arjuna said: O infallible one, please draw my chariot between the two armies so that I may see those present here, who desire to fight, and with whom I must contend in this great trial of arms.
    Purport

    Although Lord Kṛṣṇa is the Supreme Personality of Godhead, out of His causeless mercy He was engaged in the service of His friend. He never fails in His affection for His devotees, and thus He is addressed herein as infallible. As charioteer, He had to carry out the orders of Arjuna, and since He did not hesitate to do so, He is addressed as infallible. Although He had accepted the position of a charioteer for His devotee, His supreme position was not challenged. In all circumstances, He is the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Hṛṣīkeśa, the Lord of the total senses. The relationship between the Lord and His servitor is very sweet and transcendental. The servitor is always ready to render service to the Lord, and, similarly, the Lord is always seeking an opportunity to render some service to the devotee. He takes greater pleasure in His pure devotee’s assuming the advantageous position of ordering Him than He does in being the giver of orders. Since He is master, everyone is under His orders, and no one is above Him to order Him. But when He finds that a pure devotee is ordering Him, He obtains transcendental pleasure, although He is the infallible master in all circumstances. As a pure devotee of the Lord, Arjuna had no desire to fight with his cousins and brothers, but he was forced to come onto the battlefield by the obstinacy of Duryodhana, who was never agreeable to any peaceful negotiation. Therefore, he was very anxious to see who the leading persons present on the battlefield were. Although there was no question of a peacemaking endeavor on the battlefield, he wanted to see them again, and to see how much they were bent upon demanding an unwanted war.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    20-23. O King, then, as the armies prepared to fight, Arjuna with Hanumān’s insignia on his flag, seeing the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra standing there, taking his bow in hand, spoke to Hṛṣīkeśa: O Acyuta please station my chariot between the two armies, so I can view at the commencement of the war those situated with a desire to fight, and those with whom I should fight. I see that those who have gathered here, desiring to please the foolish sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, are intent on fighting.
    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    20-23. O King, then, as the armies prepared to fight, Arjuna with Hanuman insignia on his flag, seeing the sons of Dhṛtrāṣṭra standing there, taking his bow in hand, spoke to Hṛṣīkeśa: O Acyuta, please station my chariot between the two armies, so I can view at the commencement of the war those standing desirous of fighting, and those with whom I should fight. I believe that those who have gathered here, desiring to please the foolish sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, are intent on fighting.
    Commentary

    Mahīpate means “O Dhṛtarāstra.” Arjuna then spoke. “O Acyuta, you do not deviate from your innate nature—from your affection for your devotee, or from your supreme power. Controlled by this quality, without fear, place my chariot according my words, the words of your devotee.” He then speaks of the purpose of doing so. ‘Place the chariot so that I can see who are situated firmly, not trembling in fear (avasthitān), who are desirous of fighting (yoddu kamān), with no desire for compromise.” “But you are fighter, not a spectator. What will be accomplished by viewing this?” “I wish to see at the beginning of the battle those friends and relatives in whose company I will fight, and those friends and relatives against whom I will fight. For that purpose, place my chariot between the two armies. ” “Out of friendship they will make peace.” “No, there will be no conciliation between the two sides. I believe (avekṣe) that they are intent on fighting (yotsyamānām). They are intent on fighting, desiring to please the son of Dhṛtarāstra who is unintelligent (durbuddheḥ), ignorant of means for his own survival (ignorant that he is going to die), even in face of this war, which does not sober his intelligence. Therefore my viewing the rival party in war has been justified. ”

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Arjuna said: O infallible one, please draw my chariot between the two armies so that I may see those present here, who desire to fight, and with whom I must contend in this great trial of arms. (cn/DS) This is a sign that something wrong is going to happen. And this verse is the first time when our attention is drawn to Lord Krsna ‑ the Supreme Personality of Godhead, so intimate with His devotee that even takes the subordinate position.

    devotee as if He were a menial servant.

    Personal Guidance
    Arjuna asks Kṛṣṇa to position him so he can see clearly — every soul needs Kṛṣṇa to draw the chariot of life into a vantage of clear vision.
    Practical Applications
    • Begin difficult tasks by asking Kṛṣṇa, in your own words, to position you for clear sight.
    • When confused, withdraw briefly and place the matter at Kṛṣṇa's feet through prayer or japa before deciding.
    • Trust that Kṛṣṇa will move your chariot toward what you most need to see — even when it is painful.
    Reflection Questions
    • Have I asked Kṛṣṇa, today, to give me clear vision over my present situation?
    • Where am I refusing to look at what Kṛṣṇa is positioning me to see?
    Analogy

    The first thing the soul asks of the Lord is not victory, not power, not blessing — but *position me where I can see*. Arjuna's only request before his collapse is for a vantage. The Gītā opens with a prayer for sight.

    Important Words
    • yotsyamānān — those who will be fighting
      Future participle of *yudh*. Same root, third form in three verses (*yuyutsavaḥ* v.1, *yoddhu-kāmān* v.22, *yotsyamānān* v.23). Vyāsa is grammatically circling the verb of fighting — desiderative, infinitive, future participle. The Gītā is announcing that the question is not *can we fight* but *what is fighting really for*.
    • avekṣe — let me see
      First-person optative of *ava-īkṣ* — to look down upon, to inspect from above. Arjuna asks for the *bird's-eye* view. The Gītā begins with the soul climbing for vantage.
    • dhārtarāṣṭrasya — for the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra
      Genitive singular — *of/for Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son*. Arjuna does not even name Duryodhana directly. He names the *father* through the son — the lineage, the family responsibility. The blind king's name keeps haunting the verses; he is the absent author of the war.
    • durbuddheḥ — evil-minded
      *Dur-* (bad) + *buddhi* (intelligence). The opposite of *dhī-matā* ("very intelligent," v.3) and *su-mati*. The Gītā's whole psychology runs on *buddhi*: a clear *buddhi* yokes the soul to dharma, a *dur-buddhi* yokes it to ruin. The diagnosis is precise.
    • cikīrṣavaḥ — wishing
      Desiderative of *kṛ* (to do, to make) — *those wishing to do*. Same root as *karma*. The Kaurava warriors are *wishing to please* Duryodhana — wishing to *do* him good. The Gītā keeps catching the heart at the moment before action: the *wish to act* is where dharma is won or lost.
    Let me see those who have come here to fight, wishing to please the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
    Purport

    It was an open secret that Duryodhana wanted to usurp the kingdom of the Pāṇḍavas by evil plans, in collaboration with his father, Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Therefore, all persons who had joined the side of Duryodhana must have been birds of the same feather. Arjuna wanted to see them on the battlefield before the fight was begun, just to learn who they were, but he had no intention of proposing peace negotiations with them. It was also a fact that he wanted to see them to make an estimate of the strength which he had to face, although he was quite confident of victory because Kṛṣṇa was sitting by his side.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    20-23. O King, then, as the armies prepared to fight, Arjuna with Hanumān’s insignia on his flag, seeing the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra standing there, taking his bow in hand, spoke to Hṛṣīkeśa: O Acyuta please station my chariot between the two armies, so I can view at the commencement of the war those situated with a desire to fight, and those with whom I should fight. I see that those who have gathered here, desiring to please the foolish sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, are intent on fighting.
    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    20-23. O King, then, as the armies prepared to fight, Arjuna with Hanuman insignia on his flag, seeing the sons of Dhṛtrāṣṭra standing there, taking his bow in hand, spoke to Hṛṣīkeśa: O Acyuta, please station my chariot between the two armies, so I can view at the commencement of the war those standing desirous of fighting, and those with whom I should fight. I believe that those who have gathered here, desiring to please the foolish sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, are intent on fighting.
    Commentary

    Mahīpate means “O Dhṛtarāstra.” Arjuna then spoke. “O Acyuta, you do not deviate from your innate nature—from your affection for your devotee, or from your supreme power. Controlled by this quality, without fear, place my chariot according my words, the words of your devotee.” He then speaks of the purpose of doing so. ‘Place the chariot so that I can see who are situated firmly, not trembling in fear (avasthitān), who are desirous of fighting (yoddu kamān), with no desire for compromise.” “But you are fighter, not a spectator. What will be accomplished by viewing this?” “I wish to see at the beginning of the battle those friends and relatives in whose company I will fight, and those friends and relatives against whom I will fight. For that purpose, place my chariot between the two armies. ” “Out of friendship they will make peace.” “No, there will be no conciliation between the two sides. I believe (avekṣe) that they are intent on fighting (yotsyamānām). They are intent on fighting, desiring to please the son of Dhṛtarāstra who is unintelligent (durbuddheḥ), ignorant of means for his own survival (ignorant that he is going to die), even in face of this war, which does not sober his intelligence. Therefore my viewing the rival party in war has been justified. ”

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Let me see those who have come here to fight, wishing to please the evil‑minded son of Dhrtarastra. (cn/DS) 'Birds of the same feather flock together.'

    Personal Guidance
    Real courage faces opposition directly — refusing to look at one's challenges is no kind of dharma.
    Practical Applications
    • Identify the difficulty you are most avoiding looking at; spend ten minutes today examining it honestly.
    • Replace fantasy ('it will resolve itself') with sober assessment.
    • When you teach or guide others, help them face the field, not flee it.
    Reflection Questions
    • What in my life am I refusing to actually see?
    • Where does avoidance masquerade as patience or detachment?
    Analogy

    A man who calls his enemy by the truth of the enemy's intent — *durbuddheḥ*, evil-minded — and yet wishes to *see* him face to face, is not yet broken. The honest naming and the steady looking belong to the same act of courage.

    Important Words
    • hṛṣīkeśaḥ — Lord Kṛṣṇa
      Same epithet as v.15 and v.20 — *lord of the senses*. Vyāsa keeps using this particular name in the context of *positioning* and *driving*. The Lord who controls all senses is now controlling the chariot — the body-image of the *senses*. The cosmology of the verse and of the Gītā align.
    • guḍākeśena — by Arjuna
      *Guḍākā* (sleep) + *īśa* (lord) — "conqueror of sleep." An Arjuna epithet meaning *one who has mastered sleep*, i.e., one whose alertness does not lapse. Vyāsa pairs *Hṛṣīkeśa* (lord of the senses) with *Guḍākeśa* (lord of sleep) — the two *īśas* face the same chariot. The greater *īśa* serves the lesser.
    • bhārata — O descendant of Bharata
      Sañjaya here addresses Dhṛtarāṣṭra as *Bhārata*. Vyāsa keeps reminding the listener: *you, too, are of Bharata's line. The dharma being discussed is yours.* The Gītā is told within a frame; the frame keeps tapping the listener on the shoulder.
    • sthāpayitvā — placing
      Absolutive of causative *sthā* — *having placed*. Same root as Arjuna's imperative *sthāpaya* (v.21). The verbal echo is exact: Arjuna said *sthāpaya*, Kṛṣṇa did *sthāpayitvā*. The Lord answers the prayer in the same verbal root with which it was made.
    • ratha - uttamam — the finest chariot
      *Ratha* (chariot) + *uttamam* (highest, supreme). The chariot is called *uttama* — the supreme one. Not because of its wood or its horses but because of who drives it. The Lord's presence is what makes a chariot supreme.
    Sañjaya said: O descendant of Bharata, having thus been addressed by Arjuna, Lord Kṛṣṇa drew up the fine chariot in the midst of the armies of both parties.
    Purport

    In this verse Arjuna is referred to as Guḍākeśa. Guḍākā means sleep, and one who conquers sleep is called guḍākeśa. Sleep also means ignorance. So Arjuna conquered both sleep and ignorance because of his friendship with Kṛṣṇa. As a great devotee of Kṛṣṇa, he could not forget Kṛṣṇa even for a moment, because that is the nature of a devotee. Either in waking or in sleep, a devotee of the Lord can never be free from thinking of Kṛṣṇa’s name, form, qualities and pastimes. Thus a devotee of Kṛṣṇa can conquer both sleep and ignorance simply by thinking of Kṛṣṇa constantly. This is called Kṛṣṇa consciousness, or samādhi. As Hṛṣīkeśa, or the director of the senses and mind of every living entity, Kṛṣṇa could understand Arjuna’s purpose in placing the chariot in the midst of the armies. Thus He did so, and spoke as follows.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    24-25. When Arjuna spoke to him thus, Hṛṣīkeśa, stationing the best of chariots between the two armies, in front of Bhīṣma, Droṇa and all the princes, spoke: See these Kurus gathered here.
    Commentary

    The Lord, Hṛṣīkeśa, though Himself the controller of everyone’s senses, was thus ordered by Arjuna, controlled just by his words. See how the Lord is controlled by prema! This is the implication of calling the Lord Hṛṣīkeśa. Here is the significance of the word Guḍākeśa. Ākeśa means Viṣṇu (ā), Brahmā (ka) and Śiva (īśa). Guḍākeśa means Arjuna who gives them (ākeśa) the experience of the sweetness of the Lord’s affection just as sugar (guḍā) gives the experience of sweetness. [Note: Literally the word would mean “He who is the sugar for Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva.”] Therefore, Guḍākeśa refers to he who, by bringing Kṛṣṇa under his control, gave Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Śiva the opportunity to experience Kṛṣṇa’s sweetness. Where the Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa, the crown jewel, source of all avatāras, being controlled by prema, followed the orders of His servant Arjuna, how could Viṣṇu, Brahmā and Śiva, His mere expansions as guṇa avatāras, show off any of their powers? Instead, they felt they had reached the pinnacle of perfection by manifesting affectionate feelings for the Lord themselves (inspired by Arjuna). The lord of the spiritual sky (Mahāviṣṇu) said:

    dvijātmamajā me yuvayor didṛkṣuṇā I brought the brāhmaṇa’s sons here because I wanted to see the two of you.

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    24-25. When Arjuna, Guḍakeśa, spoke to him thus, Hṛṣīkeśa, stationing the best of chariots between the two armies, in front of Bīṣma, Droṇa and all the princes, spoke: See these Kurus gathered here.
    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Sanjaya said: O descendant of Bharata, having thus been addressed by Arjuna, Lord Krsna drew up the fine chariot in the midst of the armies of both parties. (cn/DS) Another symbol is shown here: Arjuna's name is Gudakesa, the conquerer of sleep or ignorance. This shows that his next show of ignorance will soon be conquered by Krsna the Master of the senses.

    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa Himself drives the chariot of the surrendered soul; at every difficult juncture, He is at the reins.
    Practical Applications
    • When you feel out of control, remember that Kṛṣṇa drives the chariot of any soul who turns to Him.
    • Hand over one decision today — speak the words 'Kṛṣṇa, you decide' and act on what arises.
    • Re-read a passage where Kṛṣṇa explicitly takes care of His devotees (BG 9.22) before bed.
    Reflection Questions
    • Whose hands are on the reins of my life right now — mine, or Kṛṣṇa's?
    • Where am I trying to drive the chariot myself when Kṛṣṇa is offering to take it?
    Analogy

    Sañjaya names the moment exactly: *thus addressed, Kṛṣṇa drew up the chariot in the middle*. The Lord of the senses obeys the soul's request for vantage. This is the deepest of the Gītā's reversals: the master responds first, the disciple speaks second.

    Stories
    Kṛṣṇa as charioteer

    Before the war, Kṛṣṇa offered both sides a choice: He Himself, unarmed, on one side; or His entire Yādava army on the other. Duryodhana, choosing what he thought was strength, took the army. Arjuna, choosing what was actually strength, took Kṛṣṇa unarmed. As part of that vow, Kṛṣṇa would not fight — but He would drive Arjuna's chariot.

    So here in verse 24, the Supreme Lord of all worlds is reduced — by His own promise — to a charioteer. The position is humble in caste terms: a *sūta* is a lower role than a *kṣatriya*. The Lord takes the lower role to bring His devotee to the higher view. *Hṛṣīkeśaḥ* — the lord of the senses — drives the chariot of one set of senses, so that those senses may finally *see*.

    Important Words
    • pramukhataḥ — in front of
      *Pra-mukha* — "face-forward." Adverbial: *facing*. Kṛṣṇa positions Arjuna *face-to-face* with the elders. Not at a distance, not at an angle — *face-forward*. The Lord does not let the devotee approach hard truth obliquely.
    • mahī - kṣitām — chiefs of the world
      *Mahī* (earth) + *kṣit* (one who rules, *kṣatra*). "Earth-rulers" — kṣatriyas in their cosmic function. The whole *kṣatriya* order is gathered here. The Gītā will, in chapter 4, name dharma as something originally spoken to the *rājarṣis*; this verse silently sets the stage for that disclosure.
    • pārtha — O son of Pṛthā
      Arjuna's matronymic — *Pṛthā's son*. Pṛthā is Kuntī. Kṛṣṇa here addresses Arjuna by his mother's name (not Pāṇḍu's). Kuntī is Kṛṣṇa's own father's sister — Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa are cousins through Pṛthā. The vocative is intimate: *son of my own aunt*, calling on the family bond before the family-killing begins.
    • paśya — just behold
      Imperative of *paś* — to see. Same word Duryodhana commanded Droṇa with in v.3 (*paśya*). Kṛṣṇa now uses the same imperative to Arjuna. Duryodhana said *paśya* to incite anxiety; Kṛṣṇa says *paśya* to invite recognition. Same word, opposite dharma.
    In the presence of Bhīṣma, Droṇa and all the other chieftains of the world, the Lord said, “Just behold, Pārtha, all the Kurus assembled here.”
    Purport

    As the Supersoul of all living entities, Lord Kṛṣṇa could understand what was going on in the mind of Arjuna. The use of the word Hṛṣīkeśa in this connection indicates that He knew everything. And the word Pārtha, meaning “the son of Pṛthā, or Kuntī,” is also similarly significant in reference to Arjuna. As a friend, He wanted to inform Arjuna that because Arjuna was the son of Pṛthā, the sister of His own father Vasudeva, He had agreed to be the charioteer of Arjuna. Now what did Kṛṣṇa mean when He told Arjuna to “behold the Kurus”? Did Arjuna want to stop there and not fight? Kṛṣṇa never expected such things from the son of His aunt Pṛthā. The mind of Arjuna was thus predicted by the Lord in friendly joking.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    24-25. When Arjuna spoke to him thus, Hṛṣīkeśa, stationing the best of chariots between the two armies, in front of Bhīṣma, Droṇa and all the princes, spoke: See these Kurus gathered here.
    Commentary

    The Lord, Hṛṣīkeśa, though Himself the controller of everyone’s senses, was thus ordered by Arjuna, controlled just by his words. See how the Lord is controlled by prema! This is the implication of calling the Lord Hṛṣīkeśa. Here is the significance of the word Guḍākeśa. Ākeśa means Viṣṇu (ā), Brahmā (ka) and Śiva (īśa). Guḍākeśa means Arjuna who gives them (ākeśa) the experience of the sweetness of the Lord’s affection just as sugar (guḍā) gives the experience of sweetness. [Note: Literally the word would mean “He who is the sugar for Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva.”] Therefore, Guḍākeśa refers to he who, by bringing Kṛṣṇa under his control, gave Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Śiva the opportunity to experience Kṛṣṇa’s sweetness. Where the Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa, the crown jewel, source of all avatāras, being controlled by prema, followed the orders of His servant Arjuna, how could Viṣṇu, Brahmā and Śiva, His mere expansions as guṇa avatāras, show off any of their powers? Instead, they felt they had reached the pinnacle of perfection by manifesting affectionate feelings for the Lord themselves (inspired by Arjuna). The lord of the spiritual sky (Mahāviṣṇu) said:

    dvijātmamajā me yuvayor didṛkṣuṇā I brought the brāhmaṇa’s sons here because I wanted to see the two of you.

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    24-25. When Arjuna, Guḍakeśa, spoke to him thus, Hṛṣīkeśa, stationing the best of chariots between the two armies, in front of Bīṣma, Droṇa and all the princes, spoke: See these Kurus gathered here.
    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    In the presence of Bhisma, Drona and all the other chieftains of the world, the Lord said, Just behold, Partha, all the Kurus assembled here. (cn/DS) Krsna predicted that Arjuna would be in distress now, and in fact He wanted Arjuna to be in distress so the Bhagavad‑gita could be spoken. Obeying the order of Arjuna to drive the chariot amidst both armies, Krsna brought the chariot right in front of Bhisma and Drona (Bhisma‑drona‑pramukhatah. 'Pramukhatah' means 'right in the face'.), his grandfather and his guru. Krsna put Arjuna in front of those to whom he was the most attached.
    Study Notes — Gauranga Priya Dāsa
    Gauranga Priya Dāsa Study
    Bhakti-śāstrī Notes, ISKCON Chowpatty (2009)
    Theme

    Hundreds of millions of warriors were in the Kuru armies, yet Kṛṣṇa drove Arjuna’s chariot directly

    before Bhīṣma and Droṇa (bhīṣma-droṇa-pramukhataù). In that way Kṛṣṇa forced Arjuna to see that

    both his grandfather and his guru were determined to oppose him in battle. Kṛṣṇa thus drew out

    Arjuna’s familial attachment so that He could speak Bhagavad-gītā. Kṛṣṇa was teasing Arjuna: “It is

    only Kurus—on both sides—who are assembled.”

    Bhagavad Gita Notes

    Śrīla Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa adds this explanation of Kṛṣṇa ’s words: “‘Because you are the son of

    My father’s sister, I am going to serve as your chariot driver. But now you are about to abandon

    your desire to fight.’ Thus Kṛṣṇa jokingly implied, ‘What’s the use of looking at the enemy’s army?’”

    In this way Kṛṣṇa affirmed the thoughts in Arjuna’s mind. Sañjaya describes this scene to

    Dhṛtarāṣṭra and then goes on to name the other family members Arjuna sees before him.

    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa positions the devotee precisely where he must see — sometimes between Bhīṣma and Droṇa, in the hardest place.
    Practical Applications
    • Stop praying only for relief; begin praying for the courage to see what Kṛṣṇa places before you.
    • Trust that the difficult position you are in is intentional — there is something you are meant to learn there.
    • Take notes after a hard conversation about what you actually saw, not what you wanted to see.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where has Kṛṣṇa positioned me precisely so that I must finally face something?
    • What am I being shown that I have been postponing for years?
    Analogy

    Kṛṣṇa positions the chariot in front of Bhīṣma and Droṇa — the two men Arjuna loves most, the two he will most need to fight. He does not station the chariot opposite Duryodhana, where the heart's blow would be easier. The Lord places the devotee exactly where it will hurt.

    Stories
    Bhīṣma and Droṇa, the two beloved enemies

    Bhīṣma had cradled Arjuna as a child after Pāṇḍu's death. Droṇa had been his archery teacher — had taught him the *Brahmāstra* itself. There were no two men in the world for whom Arjuna had more love or owed more debt. And Kṛṣṇa drives the chariot to halt directly before them.

    The Lord's positioning is precise. He could have stopped anywhere along the line. He stopped *here*. The verse names *Bhīṣma-droṇa-pramukhataḥ* — in front of the grandfather and the teacher. The Mahābhārata records that this is the moment Arjuna's heart broke. Kṛṣṇa engineered the break. The Gītā is the Lord's medicine, but the wound is also His prescription.

    Important Words
    • apaśyat — he could see
      Imperfect of *paś* — same root as Kṛṣṇa's imperative *paśya* in v.25. Kṛṣṇa said *see*, and Arjuna *saw*. The mechanism of Gītā teaching is in the verb sequence: the Lord directs the gaze, the devotee then sees.
    • pitṝn — fathers
      Plural — *fathers*. The Vedic family was extended: a man had many *fathers* (his father's brothers, his teacher, the elders of the clan). The plural is not a mistake; it is the moral scale of the offence Arjuna is being asked to commit. *Pitṛ-hatyā* — the killing of fathers — is one of the worst Vedic crimes.
    • ācāryān — teachers
      Plural of *ācārya*. Same word Duryodhana used (v.2) to address Droṇa. Here Vyāsa applies the same word — in the plural — to the men Arjuna must face. Killing a teacher (*guru-hatyā*) is among the gravest sins in Vedic dharma. The Gītā does not flinch from naming this.
    • sakhīn — friends
      *Sakhi* — friend, comrade. The Gītā will later use this same word at its highest pitch: Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa are *sakhā* (BG 4.3). The word here on the battlefield carries its ordinary meaning, but the listener already knows: *Kṛṣṇa is also Arjuna's sakha*. The category is sacred and is being violated.
    • suhṛdaḥ — well-wishers
      *Su* (good) + *hṛd* (heart) — "good-hearted ones," those who wish you well. A specific Sanskrit category: not friends one shares meals with, but those who silently want the best for you. The Mahābhārata had many such on both sides; Arjuna sees them all in one glance.
    There Arjuna could see, within the midst of the armies of both parties, his fathers, grandfathers, teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, friends, and also his fathers-in-law and well-wishers.
    Purport

    On the battlefield Arjuna could see all kinds of relatives. He could see persons like Bhūriśravā, who were his father’s contemporaries, grandfathers Bhīṣma and Somadatta, teachers like Droṇācārya and Kṛpācārya, maternal uncles like Śalya and Śakuni, brothers like Duryodhana, sons like Lakṣmaṇa, friends like Aśvatthāmā, well-wishers like Kṛtavarmā, etc. He could see also the armies which contained many of his friends.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda

    Translation
    26. Arjuna saw standing there fathers, grandfathers, teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, friends, fathers-in-law and well-wishers on both sides.
    Commentary

    Putra and pautra refer to the sons and grandsons of Duryodhana and others on the opposing side.

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    26. Arjuna saw fathers, grandfathers, teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, friends, fathers-in-law and well-wishers on both sides standing there.
    Commentary

    When the Lord spoke thus, Arjuna then looked at the opposing army. This is described in a verse and a half. In the opposing army, he saw elders like Bhūriśravaḥ [Note: He was a king in the Kuru dynastya, and was killed by Sātyaki.] (pitṛṇ), grandfathers Bhīṣma and Somadatta [Note: Somadatta was the father of Bhūriśravā. He was killed by Sātyaki.] (pītāmahān), teachers like Droṇa and Kṛpā (ācāryān), maternal uncles like Śalya [Note: Śalya was the brother of Mādrī, wife of Pāṇḍu. He sided with Duryodhana and was killed by Yudhiṣṭhira.] and Śakuni [Note: Śakuni was the brother of Gāndhārī, wife of Dhṛtarāstra.] (mātulān), brothers like Duryodhana (bhratṛn), [Note: Actually they were cousins to Arjuna.] sons like Lakṣmaṇa (putrān), [Note: Lakṣmaṇa was the son of Duryodhana. He was killed by Abhimanyu, son of Arjuna.] grandsons like the sons of Lakṣmaṇa (pautrān), contemporaries of the same age such as Aśvatthāmā and Jayadratha (sakhīn) [Note: Jayadratha was a competitor for Draupadī and later tried to abduct her from the Pāṇḍavas. He had a boon that whoever made his head touch the ground would have his own head burst into a hundred pieces. Later śiva gave him the boon that he could defeat all the Pāṇḍavas except Arjuna. Arjuna defeated him by shooting and arrow which chopped off his head and sent it onto the lap of his father in meditation, who, on seeing the head threw it off his lap, and had his own head burst.] and well-wishers like Kṛtavarma and Bhagadatta [Note: Bhagadatta was a friend of Pāṇḍu and later Yudhiṣtḥira. However he fought on the side of Duryodhana. He was killed by Arjuna. Kṛtavarma sat in Yudhiṣṭhira’s court but later fought on the side of Duryodhana. He later set fire to the camp, killing the sons of the Pāṇdāvas.] (suhṛdaḥ). This description indicates that he also looked at the troops within his own army. He reviewed both the armies that were situated there (senayor ubhayor api). The verb samīkṣya (seeing) is in the next verse.

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    There Arjuna could see, within the midst of the armies of both parties, his fathers, grandfathers, teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, friends, and also his fathers‑ in‑law and well‑wishers. (cn/DS) REVIEW: The opening scenes of the battle of Kuruksetra were described and how Sanjaya was describing to Dhrtarastra what was happening in the battlefield, and first we see Duryodhana going to Dronacarya and describing the armies of the opposing side. And then, he describes his own army and Bhismadeva who is there, the valliant grandsire of both sides, blows his conchshell. After that Krsna, Arjuna and the other Pandavas and the other worriers on their side, they also blow their conchshells. And the sound of the transcendental conchshell of Krsna shatters the hearts of Dhratastra's sons. Then Arjuna after picking up his bow and arrows and just as he is prepared to fight, he asks Krsna to drive the chariot in the midst of both the armies. And Krsna, the Supreme Lord, He drives that chariot directly in front of Bhisma and Drona. And when Arjuna sees these two great warriors, his grandfather who protected him since he was a young boy and his martial‑arts' teacher, his heart becomes overflooded with compassion. He looses in this way, his desire to fight. He sees just before him, his brothers, his uncles, his friends, etc, and seeing his kinsmen, he looses completely his desire to take part in this ghastly warfare. And yet, while Arjuna is feeling like this, both armies are still lined‑up just ready to begin the trial of arms.

    Theme

    COMMON THEME: Arjuna sees all the relatives assembled on both the sides and thus overwhelmed with

    compassion, he starts speaking

    Focus of Learning

    (a) Different grades of relatives mentioned

    Grandfathers Bhisma and Somadatta; Father’s contemporaries like Bhurisrava
    Teachers like Dronacharya and Krpacharya; Maternal uncles like Salva and Sakuni
    Brothers like Duryodhana; Sons like Laksma
    Friends like Asvatthama; Well-wishers like Krtavarma etc.
    The armies containing many of his friends

    (a) Lord as Hrsikesa – Lord knows Arjuna’s mind and thus knows everything being the Supersoul of all

    living entities

    (b) Arjuna referred to as ‘Partha’ – Indicates son of aunt ‘Prtha'. Thus Krishna wants to point out:

    He became charioteer because Arjuna is son of aunt (Queen Kunti)
    Krishna said to Arjuna: “Behold the Kurus” – This phrase indicates Arjuna’s mind “Do you want to stop and not fight?”
    Krishna does not expect such cowardly action from the son of his aunt
    Mood of friendly joking expressed here.

    (a) Arjuna as Gudakesh – one who conquers sleep

    Gudaka means sleep; sleep also means ignorance
    Arjuna conquered sleep & ignorance because of friendship with Krishna
    Nature of the devotee
    Cannot forget Krishna even for a moment (Samadhi); even while walking or asleep condition
    Devotee conquers sleep and ignorance; because of constant Krishna consciousness. (This is called Samadhi)

    (b) Krishna as Hrsikesa – As director of mind and senses, He could understand Arjuna’s purpose in

    placing the chariot in the midst of the armies – “hestitation to fight”

    Personal Guidance
    Confronting our own attachments face-to-face is the first symptom of the spiritual journey beginning in earnest.
    Practical Applications
    • Make a list of the people whose disapproval most troubles you — these reveal your attachment structure.
    • Notice which relationships feel like 'mine' in a way that contracts the heart rather than expands it.
    • Bring one such attachment into prayer this week, asking Kṛṣṇa to refine it.
    Reflection Questions
    • Whose faces, lined up before me, would shake my resolve to act in dharma?
    • What attachments would I rather not look at directly?
    Analogy

    Arjuna's first sight from the chariot is not the enemy as enemy but the enemy as *family*. Fathers, grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, friends, fathers-in-law, well-wishers — the chariot has become a mirror, and the mirror shows his life.

    Important Words
    • kṛpayā — by compassion
      Instrumental of *kṛpā* — compassion, pity. A divine quality in its purified form (Kṛṣṇa's own *kṛpā* on the devotee). But here Arjuna's *kṛpā* is *bodily compassion* — pity rooted in identification with bodies, not souls. The Gītā distinguishes the two; this verse marks the lower one.
    • parayā — of a high grade
      *Paraḥ* — supreme, highest. Arjuna's compassion is *supreme*-grade — but supreme in *intensity*, not in correctness. The Gītā uses *parā* both for the Lord (*parā prakṛti*, BG 7.5) and, here, for an intensity of misplaced feeling. Intensity alone does not equal truth.
    • āviṣṭaḥ — overwhelmed
      Past participle of *ā-viś* — to enter, to be entered into. Arjuna has been *entered* by compassion as though by a possessing force. Same root as *āveśa* (possession). The Gītā recognizes that even noble emotions can *take possession* of the soul; the discipline is to be moved by them, not occupied.
    • viṣīdan — while lamenting
      Present participle of *vi-sad* — to sink, to despond. Same root as *Viṣāda-yoga*, the title of this very chapter. *Viṣāda* is the lowest psychological state in the Gītā's atlas — the necessary collapse that precedes surrender. The chapter is named for what is happening to Arjuna in this very word.
    When the son of Kuntī, Arjuna, saw all these different grades of friends and relatives, he became overwhelmed with compassion and spoke thus.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas

    Translation

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    27. The son of Kuntī, seeing all his relatives situated there, overcome with compassion and depressed, spoke as follows.
    Commentary

    The merciful Lord of all beings, desiring to deliver the universe through instructions to His dear associate, put Arjuna under illusion, making it appear that his duty to fight was against religious principles, through a distortion of the philosophy of non-violence mentioned in the śruti with mā hiṁsyāt sarva-bhūtāni: do not commit violence against any living entity. [Note: Ahiṁsan sarva bhūtāni is found in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, 8.15. Na hiṁsyāt sarva bhūtāni is quoted by Rāmānuja in 2.19 and Srīdhara Svāmī in 18.3. na hiṁsyāt sarva bhūtāni maitrayāṇa gataḥ caret is found in Mahābharata, 12.316.18.] By addressing Arjuna as the son of Kuntī (kaunteya), as the son of his father’s sister, thereby suggesting Arjuna’s kṣatriya background, lamentation and bewilderment concering his kṣatriya dharma are here suggested. Because of his extremely compassionate nature (parayā kṛpayā), he showed remorse (viṣīdan). Because of the word krpayā in the instrumental case, there is a suggestion that this mercy is an inherent and perefect quality, emphasized by the word para, superior. Through analyzing the saṅdhi differently, the word aparayā can also be formed. In that case the meaning is “Though he had previously shown compassion for those in his own army, now he also showed different compassion for the members of the opposing army (aparayā kṛpāyā).” In stating that Arjuna talked while lamenting at the same time, it is suggested that while talking he showed the effects of remorse—tears, quivering body and contracted throat.

    Personal Guidance
    Material compassion — born from bodily identification — is not real compassion; true compassion is rooted in the eternal soul.
    Practical Applications
    • Distinguish in your own reactions between sentimental compassion (avoiding others' discomfort) and real compassion (serving their eternal good).
    • Ask: would Prabhupāda call this compassion, or attachment?
    • When you feel pulled to 'protect' someone, check if you are protecting their soul or their body.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where is my 'compassion' actually a refusal to do what dharma requires?
    • Whom am I 'sparing' from a truth they need to hear?
    Analogy

    Compassion (*kṛpā*) is a fine thing — but compassion mixed with confusion is a paralysis disguised as virtue. Arjuna is *overwhelmed* (*āviṣṭa*) by compassion the way a swimmer is overwhelmed by a wave: it does not save him; it takes him under.

    Important Words
    • sva - janam — kinsmen
      *Sva* (one's own) + *jana* (person). Literally *one's own people*. Same root *sva-* that runs through *svadharma*, *svabhāva*, *svarūpa*. Arjuna sees the enemy and his eye registers *sva-jana* — *mine*. The pronoun-error of verse 1 (*māmakāḥ*) now repeats in Arjuna's mouth. The Gītā treats both sides as suffering from the same illusion.
    • yuyutsum — all in a fighting spirit
      Desiderative of *yudh* — fourth recurrence of this root in the chapter (vv.1, 22, 23, 28). Vyāsa wants the auditor to feel the rhythm of *yudh, yudh, yudh*. Then suddenly Arjuna's body announces: I no longer have it.
    • sīdanti — are quivering
      Same root *sad* (to sink) as *viṣīdan* (v.27). The body is *sinking*. Vyāsa is layering the *sad*-root: psychological *viṣāda* (v.27) becomes physical *sīdana* (v.28). The Gītā traces the descent of an inner state into the body.
    • gātrāṇi — limbs of the body
      *Gātra* — a limb, a body-part. From *gam* (to go) — that which *goes*, that which moves. The mobile body is becoming immobile. The instrument of action is refusing the verb of action. The Gītā will later teach that the body is meant to *go* in dharma; when it cannot go in adharma, that is health, not weakness.
    • pariśuṣyati — is drying up
      *Pari-* (around, completely) + *śuṣ* (to dry). Total drying. The same root as *śuṣka* (dry, withered). Arjuna's mouth is going through what the Vedic tradition names as a classical sign of intense fear — drying of the saliva, drying of the inner channels. The body is in *vairāgya* against the act it is being asked to do.
    Arjuna said: My dear Kṛṣṇa, seeing my friends and relatives present before me in such a fighting spirit, I feel the limbs of my body quivering and my mouth drying up.
    Purport

    Any man who has genuine devotion to the Lord has all the good qualities which are found in godly persons or in the demigods, whereas the nondevotee, however advanced he may be in material qualifications by education and culture, lacks in godly qualities. As such, Arjuna, just after seeing his kinsmen, friends and relatives on the battlefield, was at once overwhelmed by compassion for them who had so decided to fight amongst themselves. As far as his soldiers were concerned, he was sympathetic from the beginning, but he felt compassion even for the soldiers of the opposite party, foreseeing their imminent death. And while he was so thinking, the limbs of his body began to quiver, and his mouth became dry. He was more or less astonished to see their fighting spirit. Practically the whole community, all blood relatives of Arjuna, had come to fight with him. This overwhelmed a kind devotee like Arjuna. Although it is not mentioned here, still one can easily imagine that not only were Arjuna’s bodily limbs quivering and his mouth drying up, but he was also crying out of compassion. Such symptoms in Arjuna were not due to weakness but to his softheartedness, a characteristic of a pure devotee of the Lord. It is said therefore: yasyāsti bhaktir bhagavaty akiñcanā sarvair guṇais tatra samāsate surāḥ harāv abhaktasya kuto mahad-guṇā mano-rathenāsati dhāvato bahiḥ “One who has unflinching devotion for the Personality of Godhead has all the good qualities of the demigods. But one who is not a devotee of the Lord has only material qualifications that are of little value. This is because he is hovering on the mental plane and is certain to be attracted by the glaring material energy.” ( Bhāg. 5.18.12 )

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    28-29. O Kṛṣṇa, seeing all my relatives and friends gathered to fight, my limbs are weakening, my mouth is drying up, my body is trembling and my hairs are standing on end. My bow is falling from my hand and my skin is burning.
    Commentary

    Seeing all these known people, my mouth has dried up. The phrase “As I stand here” should be added at the beginning of the sentence. “As I stand here seeing this, my limbs become weak.”

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    28-29. O Kṛṣṇa, seeing all my relatives and friends gathered to fight, my limbs are weakening, my mouth is drying up, my body is trembling and my hairs are standing on end. My bow is falling from my hand and my skin is burning.
    Commentary

    Having been described as afflicted with lamentation, Arjuna in this verse expresses the same in his speaking. Svajanam, meaning his group of friends, is in the singular case to express a class. Amara Kośa says that svajana is the equivalent of friend or relative. After I, situated here, have seen those relatives assembled, my limbs such as hands and feet are weakening (sīdanti), and my mouth has dried up completely (pariśuṣyati) from fatigue. His hairs were standing on end (roma harṣaḥ) and his body was quivering (vepathuḥ). That his bow was falling from his hand indicated his unsteadiness, and his burning skin indicated his burning heart.

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Arjuna said: My dear Krsna, seeing my friends and relatives present before me in such a fighting spirit, I feel the limbs of my body quivering and my mouth drying up. (cn/DS) These were people that he grew up with. Naturally so much affection, was in his heart, for all these people ‑ and there they were, to keep the kingdom for themselves, they wanted to fight and kill. But would Arjuna, such a softhearted devotee, wanted to do such a foolish thing? To kill so many, to commit unlimited sins, just to get a kingdom?

    PRACTICAL APPLICATION OF SECTION II

    Identification with, and attachment to the body disables one from executing his religious duties, which is ultimately to execute Krishna’s will
    It is interesting to analyze the cause and effect of Arjuna’s bewilderment
    It is brought on by seeing in terms of one’s own self-interest
    The result of such vision is fear, loss of composure, indecision, and confusion of moral codes

    Personal Guidance
    When the soul awakens to the gravity of bodily existence, the body itself trembles — these are early symptoms of spiritual seriousness.
    Practical Applications
    • Honor the moments of inner shaking; they often signal a deeper layer of the heart preparing to open.
    • When you feel emotionally overwhelmed by a moral question, take it as Kṛṣṇa's invitation to a higher dharma.
    • Avoid medicating spiritual discomfort with entertainment; sit with it in front of the deity or with japa.
    Reflection Questions
    • When did I last feel my limbs shake at the weight of a real choice?
    • What am I numbing instead of letting Kṛṣṇa awaken?
    Analogy

    The body knows what the mind has not yet admitted. Arjuna's limbs are quivering and his mouth has gone dry — the soldier's instrument is already announcing surrender before the soldier himself can speak it.
