    Translation
    1.40 Sri Sankaracharya did not comment on this sloka. The commentary starts from 2.10.
    Śrī Rāmānujācārya Classical
    Translation
    1.26 - 1.47 Arjuna said - Sanjaya said Sanjaya continued: The high-minded Arjuna, extremely kind, deeply friendly, and supremely righteous, having brothers like himself, though repeatedly deceived by the treacherous attempts of your people like burning in the lac-house etc., and therefore fit to be killed by him with the help of the Supreme Person, nevertheless said, 'I will not fight.' He felt weak, overcome as he was by his love and extreme compassion for his relatives. He was also filled with fear, not knowing what was righteous and what unrighteous. His mind was tortured by grief, because of the thought of future separation from his relations. So he threw away his bow and arrow and sat on the chariot as if to fast to death.
    Śrī Abhinavagupta Classical
    Translation
    1.35 1.44 Nihatya etc. upto anususruma. Sin alone is the agent in the act of slaying these desperadoes. Therefore here the idea is this : These ememies of ours have been slain, i.e., have been take possession of, by sin. Sin would come to us also after slaying them. Sin in this context is the disregard, on account of greed etc., to the injurious conseences like the ruination of the family and the like. That is why Arjuna makes a specific mention of the [ruin of the] family etc., and of its duties in the passage 'How by slaying my own kinsmen etc'. The act of slaying, undertaken with an individualizing idea about its result, and with a particularizing idea about the person to be slain, is a great sin. To say this very thing precisely and to indicate the intensity of his own agony, Arjuna says only to himself [see next sloka]:

    Personal Guidance
    The destruction of dharma in a family is the destruction of the family itself; the surface form survives, but the soul of the lineage is gone.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice the difference between maintaining a family's outer customs and maintaining its dharma.
    • Have one explicitly spiritual conversation with a family member this month.
    • Do not let economic concerns silently displace the religious heart of your home.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where have we kept the form of family but lost its dharma?
    • What am I willing to do to restore the spiritual current of my lineage?
    Analogy

    When the household lamp is extinguished, the moths fly elsewhere. Without the protections that *dharma* gives the home, the women — who carry the future of the lineage in their bodies — are the first to be exposed to corruption. The verse names the social physics: the dignity of women rises and falls with the dharma of the men.

    Stories
    Draupadī in the dice-hall

    Years before Kurukṣetra, in this very Kuru court, Yudhiṣṭhira had gambled away his kingdom, his brothers, himself, and finally Draupadī. Duḥśāsana dragged her by the hair into the assembly, attempted to disrobe her, and the elders of the family — Bhīṣma included — sat silent. Kṛṣṇa alone, unseen, extended her sari endlessly.

    Arjuna saw this. He had been present, bound by his elder's pledge, watching his wife humiliated by his cousins. *Strīṣu duṣṭāsu vārṣṇeya jāyate varṇa-saṅkaraḥ* — "O descendant of Vṛṣṇi, from women being so afflicted, mixed-up society is born." When he says these words on the chariot, he is remembering the dice-hall. The verse is not theory for him — it is biography. The *kula-dharma* of the Kurus had already failed once, in his own life. The war is the consequence of that earlier failure.

    Important Words
    • saṅkaraḥ — such unwanted children
      *Saṅkara* repeated from v.40 — the mixed offspring of broken *varṇa* boundaries. The compound names a category of social and ritual disorder. Vyāsa is letting Arjuna develop the doctrine with technical accuracy; the diagnosis is correct, the prescription will be corrected.
    • narakāya — make for hellish life
      *Naraka* — the technical Vedic underworlds. Dative case — *for the purpose of hell*. Arjuna's eschatology is specific: family-destroyers fall into *naraka*. The Gītā will not deny *naraka* (BG 16.16 confirms it) but will redefine the path away from it — surrender to Kṛṣṇa, not abstention from duty.
    • kula - ghnānām — for those who are killers of the family
      *Kula* + *ghna* (slayer, from *han*). Genitive plural. Same *han*-root that the chapter is saturated with. Arjuna names *kula-ghna* as a class — those who *slay the family*. He is afraid of being categorized under this noun. The Gītā will teach that *not* fighting in this war is what makes one a *kula-ghna* — by allowing adharma to take over.
    • piṇḍa — offerings of food
      *Piṇḍa* — the rice-ball offered to ancestors in *śrāddha* rites. Technical Vedic ritual term. The *piṇḍa* sustains the *pitṛs* in the *pitṛ-loka*. Without the *piṇḍa*, ancestors fall. Vedic religion is a system of *vertical reciprocity* between the living and the dead; *kula-kṣaya* breaks the system.
    • udaka — offerings of water
      *Udaka* — the water libations also given in *śrāddha*. Together with the *piṇḍa*, the *udaka* makes the ancestor offering complete. The two words together name the full ritual. Arjuna's fear is technically precise: the entire *śrāddha* mechanism would lapse. The Gītā does not deny the importance of *śrāddha*; it teaches that surrender to Kṛṣṇa fulfils all such obligations at once (BG 18.66).
    An increase of unwanted population certainly causes hellish life both for the family and for those who destroy the family tradition. The ancestors of such corrupt families fall down, because the performances for offering them food and water are entirely stopped.
    Purport

    According to the rules and regulations of fruitive activities, there is a need to offer periodical food and water to the forefathers of the family. This offering is performed by worship of Viṣṇu, because eating the remnants of food offered to Viṣṇu can deliver one from all kinds of sinful reactions. Sometimes the forefathers may be suffering from various types of sinful reactions, and sometimes some of them cannot even acquire a gross material body and are forced to remain in subtle bodies as ghosts. Thus, when remnants of prasādam food are offered to forefathers by descendants, the forefathers are released from ghostly or other kinds of miserable life. Such help rendered to forefathers is a family tradition, and those who are not in devotional life are required to perform such rituals. One who is engaged in the devotional life is not required to perform such actions. Simply by performing devotional service, one can deliver hundreds and thousands of forefathers from all kinds of misery. It is stated in the Bhāgavatam (11.5.41) : devarṣi-bhūtāpta-nṛṇāṁ pitṝṇāṁ na kiṅkaro nāyam ṛṇī ca rājan sarvātmanā yaḥ śaraṇaṁ śaraṇyaṁ gato mukundaṁ parihṛtya kartam “Anyone who has taken shelter of the lotus feet of Mukunda, the giver of liberation, giving up all kinds of obligation, and has taken to the path in all seriousness, owes neither duties nor obligations to the demigods, sages, general living entities, family members, humankind or forefathers.” Such obligations are automatically fulfilled by performance of devotional service to the Supreme Personality of Godhead.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    41. Mixed caste in the family brings hell for those who have destroyed their family members. The forefathers fall, being deprived of piṇḍa and water offerings.
    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    41. Mixed caste in the family brings hell for those who have destroyed their family members. Moreover the forefathers fall to hell, being deprived of piṇḍa and water offerings.
    Commentary

    The mixture of caste in the family leads to hell for those who destroy the family and its traditions. Not only do they go to hell, but because of this (hi indicates “reason”) the ancestors of the family (pitaraḥ) also fall to hell because of being deprived of the piṇḍa offerings from lack of sons who are qualified givers of piṇḍa.

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    An increase of unwanted population certainly causes hellish life both for the family and for those who destroy the family tradition. The ancestors of such corrupt families fall down, because the performances for offering them food and water are entirely stopped. (cn/DS) Even Lord Caitanya offered 'sraddha' ceremony for His father in Gaya. We can't think that this is just superficial, that we are vaisnavas, that is not important to perform these things. This is very important for the entire culture. The ancestors are dependent on these types of sacrifices to become free from all types of sufferings.

    Gauranga Priya Dāsa Study
    Bhakti-śāstrī Notes, ISKCON Chowpatty (2009)
    Theme

    COMMON THEME: Fighting will cause family destruction in the following 6-step sequence:

    1. Death of Elderly (1.39)

    Fighting destroys the whole dynasty

    2. Family Traditions Stop: Irreligion increases (1.39)

    With the destruction of dynasty, the entire family tradition is vanquished, and thus the rest of the family becomes involved in irreligion

    3. Women polluted (1.40)

    When irreligion is prominent, the women in the family become polluted
    Chanakya Pandit says “Women need protection”
    Why women need special protection – Because they are
    Less intelligent
    Not trustworthy
    Prone to degradation
    How they are protected – By engaging in religious principles, either under father, husband or son
    If they are not protected, it leads to adultery and varna-sankara

    4. Varna-sankara (unwanted progeny) (1.40*)

    From degradation of woman comes unwanted progeny
    Varna-sankara has three effects
    Risk of war and pestilence
    Hellish life
    For the whole family – Ancestors falldown because pinda-dana stops

    ▪

    For those who destroy family

    All community projects and family welfare acts stop

    5. Hellish life for ‘family’ and ‘destroyers of family’ (1.41*)

    6. Culture is destroyed – Community projects and family welfare acts stop (1.42)

    Focus of Learning

    (c) Correct understanding about forgiveness / saintliness

    Saintliness is not justified for a ksatriya
    Compared to “Rama-rajya” – Lord Rama gave sufficient lessons to Ravana who was an aggressor because he kidnapped Rama’s wife, Mother Sita

    (d) ‘Madhava’ – Arjuna addresses Krishna as ‘Madhava’ to indicate:

    Krishna is the husband of the Goddess of ‘fortune’
    Krishna should not cause an action which brings ‘misfortune’

    (e) Saintliness of Arjuna – Arjuna’s thorough consideration of evil consequences reveals saintliness

    (1.37 – 1.38)

    Obligation (To not refuse when challenged to battle or gamble) is binding when the effect is good, not otherwise
    Therefore Arjuna considered that he is not obliged to fight
    ARJUNA’S FIFTH ARGUMENT — “INDECISION”

    FIFTH ARGUMENT COVERED IN CHAPTER 2:

    Please refer to Text 2.6 for Arjuna’s fifth argument

    PLEASE NOTE: Some points of the purport are covered in the ‘6-step sequence of family destruction’

    theme above

    (a) Varnashrama Institution (1.39 purport) – Principles of religious traditions to help members of

    family grow and attain spiritual values

    (b) Role of elders (1.39 purport)

    Responsible for maintaining purificatory samskaras (birth to death)
    Helping younger generation on the path of salvation

    (c) Importance of good population (1.40 purport) – It is the basic principle for peace, prosperity and

    spiritual progress in life

    (d) What good population depends on (1.40 purport) – Chastity and faithfulness of womanhood

    (e) Philosophy of Pinda-Dan (1.41 purport)

    Based on rules and regulations of fruitive acts
    What it is – To offer periodical food and water to forefathers
    Right process – worship of Vishnu done / remnants offered to forefathers
    Principle: To release them from many sinful reactions / ghostly existence etc.
    Who is not obliged for this – One in devotional life
    Why devotees are not obliged – Because devotional service relieves hundreds and thousands of forefathers from all misery (Ref. SB. 11.5.41 “devarsi bhutapta…”)

    (f) Community projects and family welfare acts – Importance (1.42 purport)

    They are set forth by Varnashrama / Sanatana-dharma
    Sets duties for four orders of society
    Purpose – To help attain ultimate salvation
    ‘Result of breaking’ such projects
    Chaos in society
    People forget ultimate aim of life – Vishnu

    (g) Ways of receiving real knowledge (1.43 purport) – Disciplic succession

    Arjuna based his arguments not on personal experience, but on what he has heard from authorities

    (h) Principle of ‘Prayascitta’ (1.43 purport) – A system in the varnashrama system by which before

    death one has to undergo the process of atonement for his sinful activities

    Without doing so, one surely will be transferred to the hellish planets to undergo miserable lives
    Classical Ācāryas
    Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Classical
    Translation
    1.41 Sri Sankaracharya did not comment on this sloka. The commentary starts from 2.10.
    Śrī Rāmānujācārya Classical
    Translation
    1.26 - 1.47 Arjuna said - Sanjaya said Sanjaya continued: The high-minded Arjuna, extremely kind, deeply friendly, and supremely righteous, having brothers like himself, though repeatedly deceived by the treacherous attempts of your people like burning in the lac-house etc., and therefore fit to be killed by him with the help of the Supreme Person, nevertheless said, 'I will not fight.' He felt weak, overcome as he was by his love and extreme compassion for his relatives. He was also filled with fear, not knowing what was righteous and what unrighteous. His mind was tortured by grief, because of the thought of future separation from his relations. So he threw away his bow and arrow and sat on the chariot as if to fast to death.
    Śrī Abhinavagupta Classical
    Translation
    1.35 1.44 Nihatya etc. upto anususruma. Sin alone is the agent in the act of slaying these desperadoes. Therefore here the idea is this : These ememies of ours have been slain, i.e., have been take possession of, by sin. Sin would come to us also after slaying them. Sin in this context is the disregard, on account of greed etc., to the injurious conseences like the ruination of the family and the like. That is why Arjuna makes a specific mention of the [ruin of the] family etc., and of its duties in the passage 'How by slaying my own kinsmen etc'. The act of slaying, undertaken with an individualizing idea about its result, and with a particularizing idea about the person to be slain, is a great sin. To say this very thing precisely and to indicate the intensity of his own agony, Arjuna says only to himself [see next sloka]:
    Swami Sivananda Classical
    Translation
    1.41. By the prevalence of impiety, O Krishna, the women of the family become corrupt; and , women being corrupted, O Varshenya (descendant of Vrishni), there arises intermingling of castes.
    Commentary

    1.41 अधर्माभिभवात् from the prevalence of impiety? कृष्ण O Krishna? प्रदुष्यन्ति become corrupt? कुलस्त्रियः the women of the family? स्त्रीषु in women? दुष्टासु (being) corrupt? वार्ष्णेय O Varshneya? जायते arises? वर्णसङ्करः casteadmixture.No Commentary.

    Swami Gambhīrānanda Classical
    Translation
    1.41 O Krsna, when vice predominates, the women of the family become corrupt. O descendent of the Vrsnis, when women become corrupted, it results in the intermingling of castes.
    Shri Purohit Swami Classical
    Translation
    1.41 When irreligion spreads, the women of the house begin to stray; when they lose their purity, adulteration of the stock follows.

    Personal Guidance
    When dharma weakens, women — and the values associated with the feminine principle — suffer first; protect the conditions that allow purity and dignity.
    Practical Applications
    • Examine how your home and community honor the feminine in its full spiritual dignity.
    • Resist cultural currents that reduce women (or any soul) to objects of exploitation.
    • Speak up when conversations or media in your circle degrade the feminine principle.
    Reflection Questions
    • What does my environment communicate to the women in it about their spiritual worth?
    • Where do I tolerate cultural degradation that I should refuse?
    Analogy

    When the rituals that link the living to the ancestors are interrupted, the dead drift. The Vedic worldview is dense with downward causation: the *piṇḍa* and *udaka* offerings sustain the *pitṛs*. A society that forgets its ritual obligations starves its own forebears.

    Word-for-word
    doṣaiḥ — by such faults etaiḥ — all these kula - ghnānām — of the destroyers of the family varṇa - saṅkara — of unwanted children kārakaiḥ — which are causes utsādyante — are devastated jāti - dharmāḥ — community projects kula - dharmāḥ — family traditions ca — also śāśvatāḥ — eternal .
    Blended reading (Sanskrit + English inline)
    doṣair etaiḥ kula-ghnānāṁ
    doṣaiḥ
    by such faults
    etaiḥ
    all these
    kula - ghnānām
    of the destroyers of the family

    Important Words
    • doṣaiḥ — by such faults
      *Doṣa* (v.37–38) returns — now in the instrumental plural, as *the agency* by which destruction occurs. Same root *duṣ-* (to spoil) as *duṣṭa* (corrupt) and *Kāli-yuga*'s *duṣṭam*. The verse is naming *doṣa* as a self-propagating force.
    • kula - ghnānām — of the destroyers of the family
      Same compound as v.41, repeated. Arjuna keeps applying this label to himself by anticipation. The Gītā will eventually relieve him of this anxiety by showing that the *true* preservation of the *kula* requires the discharge of his duty, not its abandonment.
    • kārakaiḥ — which are causes
      *Kāraka* — agent, cause. From *kṛ* — to do, to make. Same root as *karma*. *Kāraka* is also a technical grammatical term: the syntactic relation a word bears to an action (agent, instrument, object, etc.). The unwanted progeny become *kārakas* — *agents* — of further destruction. Adharma propagates by producing new agents of itself.
    • jāti - dharmāḥ — community projects
      *Jāti* (birth, community) + *dharma*. The *community-level* dharmas, broader than the *kula*. The verse hierarchizes: *kula-dharma* is the family unit; *jāti-dharma* is the community unit. Arjuna sees both collapsing. The Gītā will eventually transcend both with *bhakti-dharma* (BG 9.32), open to all *jātis*.
    • śāśvatāḥ — eternal
      *Śāśvata* — perpetual, abiding. A close synonym of *sanātana* (v.39). The Gītā uses *śāśvata* repeatedly for the soul (BG 2.20, 11.18) and for Kṛṣṇa (BG 10.12). Arjuna applies *śāśvata* to *kula-dharma*. The Gītā will gently relocate the adjective onto the soul itself: the only truly *śāśvata* thing is the *ātman*.
    By the evil deeds of those who destroy the family tradition and thus give rise to unwanted children, all kinds of community projects and family welfare activities are devastated.
    Purport

    Community projects for the four orders of human society, combined with family welfare activities, as they are set forth by the institution of sanātana-dharma, or varṇāśrama-dharma, are designed to enable the human being to attain his ultimate salvation. Therefore, the breaking of the sanātana-dharma tradition by irresponsible leaders of society brings about chaos in that society, and consequently people forget the aim of life – Viṣṇu. Such leaders are called blind, and persons who follow such leaders are sure to be led into chaos.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    42. Both caste and family rules are destroyed by this fault of mixed varṇas caused by the killers of family members.
    Commentary

    By the faults of mixture of castes, both the caste rules and the family rules will be destroyed (utsādyate).

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    42. Both caste and traditional family rules are destroyed by this fault of mixed varṇas caused by the killers of family members.
    Commentary

    In two verses, Arjuna summarizes the faults. The principles of being a kṣatriya (jāti dharma) and the principles and special rules of the particular family (kula dharma), and āśrāma principles as well (ca), will disappear (utsādyante).

    Personal Guidance
    Without the offerings and remembrances rooted in dharma, the lineage of souls — past, present, and future — loses its anchor.
    Practical Applications
    • Maintain regular remembrance of departed family members through Vaiṣṇava means (offering prasāda, chanting, śrāddha).
    • Treat your gṛhastha responsibilities as worship, not as competing with worship.
    • Pass on at least one spiritual practice to the next generation — not as duty but as gift.
    Reflection Questions
    • How am I caring for the lineage of souls that came before me?
    • What spiritual gift am I leaving for those who come after?
    Analogy

    Arjuna is now naming the chain of consequence in full: family-destroyers → mixed offspring → loss of *jāti-dharma* → loss of *kula-dharma*. The logic is air-tight as dharma-sociology. What is missing is only the higher principle that the Gītā will reveal: *Kṛṣṇa Himself is the maintainer of dharma; refusing one's duty does not preserve dharma — it abandons it to Him to repair alone*.

    Important Words
    • utsanna — spoiled
      *Ut-sad* — to be uprooted, to be spoiled. Same root *sad-* (to sink, to settle) that produced *viṣīda* (v.27) and *sīdanti* (v.28). Vyāsa keeps weaving this root through the chapter. *Sad-* is the underlying physics of the whole *viṣāda-yoga* — things keep *settling, sinking, being uprooted*.
    • manuṣyāṇām — of such men
      *Manuṣya* — human being. From *manu* (the first man) — same root as *manas* (mind). Sanskrit's word for human is *the one with mind*. Arjuna names humans through the mind-faculty; the Gītā will spend chapters disciplining precisely the *manas* of *manuṣya*.
    • narake — in hell
      *Naraka* — the Vedic underworlds, repeated from v.41. Arjuna doubles down: *eternally* in *naraka*. The Gītā does not contradict the cosmology; it offers the way out of it (BG 9.30–32: *even the worst sinner, if turning to Me, is to be considered righteous*).
    • anuśuśruma — I have heard by disciplic succession
      First-person plural perfect of *anu-śru* — to hear *along*, to hear *after* a teacher. The technical Vedic word for *received tradition*. Arjuna invokes *paramparā* to justify his refusal. The Gītā's response in chapter 4 will be precisely this: *evaṁ paramparā-prāptam* — this knowledge was lost; I am restoring the paramparā by speaking it to you now. The very tradition Arjuna invokes is being re-spoken by its source.
    O Kṛṣṇa, maintainer of the people, I have heard by disciplic succession that those whose family traditions are destroyed dwell always in hell.
    Purport

    Arjuna bases his argument not on his own personal experience, but on what he has heard from the authorities. That is the way of receiving real knowledge. One cannot reach the real point of factual knowledge without being helped by the right person who is already established in that knowledge. There is a system in the varṇāśrama institution by which before death one has to undergo the process of atonement for his sinful activities. One who is always engaged in sinful activities must utilize the process of atonement, called prāyaścitta. Without doing so, one surely will be transferred to hellish planets to undergo miserable lives as the result of sinful activities.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda

We have heard from the mouth of the guru (anuśuśruma) about this, with such words as the following: prāyaścittam akurvāṇāḥ pāpeṣu niratā narāḥ apaścāt-tāpinaḥ kaṣṭān nirayān yānti dāruṇān Those who do not perform prāyaścittas after engaging in sins, and are not repentant, go to the most terrible hells. [Note: This is quoted by Śrīdhara Svāmī.]

    All community projects and family welfare acts stop

    5. Hellish life for ‘family’ and ‘destroyers of family’ (1.41*)

    6. Culture is destroyed – Community projects and family welfare acts stop (1.42)

    Focus of Learning

    (c) Correct understanding about forgiveness / saintliness

    Saintliness is not justified for a ksatriya
    Compared to “Rama-rajya” – Lord Rama gave sufficient lessons to Ravana who was an aggressor because he kidnapped Rama’s wife, Mother Sita

    (d) ‘Madhava’ – Arjuna addresses Krishna as ‘Madhava’ to indicate:

    Krishna is the husband of the Goddess of ‘fortune’
    Krishna should not cause an action which brings ‘misfortune’

    Therefore Arjuna considered that he is not obliged to fight

    Śrī Rāmānujācārya Classical
    Translation
    1.26 - 1.47 Arjuna said - Sanjaya said Sanjaya continued: The high-minded Arjuna, extremely kind, deeply friendly, and supremely righteous, having brothers like himself, though repeatedly deceived by the treacherous attempts of your people like burning in the lac-house etc., and therefore fit to be killed by him with the help of the Supreme Person, nevertheless said, 'I will not fight.' He felt weak, overcome as he was by his love and extreme compassion for his relatives. He was also filled with fear, not knowing what was righteous and what unrighteous. His mind was tortured by grief, because of the thought of future separation from his relations. So he threw away his bow and arrow and sat on the chariot as if to fast to death.
    Śrī Abhinavagupta Classical
    Translation
    1.35 1.44 Nihatya etc. upto anususruma. Sin alone is the agent in the act of slaying these desperadoes. Therefore here the idea is this : These ememies of ours have been slain, i.e., have been take possession of, by sin. Sin would come to us also after slaying them. Sin in this context is the disregard, on account of greed etc., to the injurious conseences like the ruination of the family and the like. That is why Arjuna makes a specific mention of the [ruin of the] family etc., and of its duties in the passage 'How by slaying my own kinsmen etc'. The act of slaying, undertaken with an individualizing idea about its result, and with a particularizing idea about the person to be slain, is a great sin. To say this very thing precisely and to indicate the intensity of his own agony, Arjuna says only to himself [see next sloka]:

    Personal Guidance
    The destruction of caste-dharma — the systematic structures that allow each soul to do its proper work — leaves society leaderless and disordered.
    Practical Applications
    • Honor the natural varṇāśrama tendencies in yourself and others rather than forcing everyone into the same role.
    • Recognize the contribution of each devotee's nature; do not demand they all become like you.
    • Build community structures that allow brāhmaṇical, kṣatriya, vaiśya, and śūdra natures to all serve Kṛṣṇa.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where am I trying to force everyone into one mold rather than honoring different natures?
    • How might my community better serve the diversity of Vaiṣṇava temperaments?
    Analogy

    Arjuna invokes tradition (*anuśuśruma* — "we have heard by disciplic succession") to support his refusal. But to claim *paramparā* against the personal instruction of Kṛṣṇa Himself, who *is* the source of the *paramparā* (BG 4.1–3), is to use the river's water to argue against the river's spring. The Gītā will not deny tradition; it will reseat tradition in its true source.

    Important Words
    • aho — alas
      Emphatic particle of dismay, formally paired with the *bata* that follows. A standard Sanskrit exclamation used at moments of moral self-recognition. Arjuna is performing the *aho-bata* gesture of a man catching himself in time, surprised by his own conclusions.
    • bata — how strange it is
      The companion of *aho* — "alas, alas!" Together they form one of the strongest expressions of self-rebuke in classical Sanskrit. Yudhiṣṭhira will use this very pair when he sees his brothers fallen in the *yakṣa-praśna* episode. Arjuna's reflexive surprise at his own posture is the verse's hinge.
    • mahat — great
      *Mahat* — great, of grand scale. Same word the Gītā will use for *mahat-tattva* (the cosmic intelligence-principle, BG 14.3). Here it modifies *pāpa*: *great sin*. Arjuna is sizing the offence correctly. The Gītā will not minimize the sin; it will show how the offence is to be discharged in dharma rather than evaded.
    • vyavasitāḥ — have decided
      Past passive participle of *vi-ava-sā* — to determine, to resolve. Same root as *vyavasāya* (resolution), which the Gītā praises in 2.41: *vyavasāyātmikā buddhir ekā* — "the resolute intellect is one." Arjuna says "we have *vyavasita* — we have resolved — to do a great sin." The same verb of resolution that the Gītā will commend can also resolve toward catastrophe; the verb is neutral, the *direction* matters.
    • rājya - sukha - lobhena — driven by greed for royal happiness
      Triple compound: *rājya* (kingdom) + *sukha* (happiness) + *lobha* (greed). Instrumental case. Arjuna correctly names the three: kingdom-greed, happiness-greed, and *lobha* itself as the underlying force. The same *lobha* he attributed to the Kauravas in v.37. Now he attributes it to himself. Self-honesty rising.
    • udyatāḥ — trying
      Past participle of *ud-yam* — to lift up, to be in readiness. Same root as Arjuna's earlier *udyamya* (v.20) — "taking up the bow." In v.20 he *lifted the bow*; here he is *lifted toward the sin*. The verb of exertion is morally neutral until the object is named.
    Alas, how strange it is that we are preparing to commit greatly sinful acts. Driven by the desire to enjoy royal happiness, we are intent on killing our own kinsmen.
    Purport

    Driven by selfish motives, one may be inclined to such sinful acts as the killing of one’s own brother, father or mother. There are many such instances in the history of the world. But Arjuna, being a saintly devotee of the Lord, is always conscious of moral principles and therefore takes care to avoid such activities.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    44. We are intent on committing great sin, since we are ready to kill our own people for gain of happiness of a kingdom.
    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    44. We are certain to commit great sin, since we are ready to kill our own people for gain of happiness of a kingdom.
    Commentary

    In this verse he speaks about the sin in even thinking of yet uncommitted killing of relatives . Bata here indicates the great danger.

    SUMMARISED THEME 1A
    ARJUNA’S SAINTLINESS REVEALED (1.28 — 1.46)

    Arjuna’s saintliness is revealed by the following points:

    (a) Softheartedness (1.28)

    (b) Does not want to kill even for exchange of three worlds (1.35)

    (c) Ready to forgive any aggressors (1.36)

    (d) Considers evil consequences even at the risk of refusing obligation to fight (1.37 – 1.38)

    (e) Conscious of obligations to protect family traditions and morals (1.39 – 1.44)

    He does not think that: “I am transcendental and I have no obligations”
    Arjuna being saintly is conscious of moral principles – How he can kill one’s relatives based on selfish motives (1.44)

    (f) Ready to be killed unarmed, but not retaliate (1.45)

    Custom according to Ksatriya fighting principles – unarmed and unwilling foe should not be attacked
    These symptoms are due to softheartedness resulting from being a great devotee

    (g) Kept his bow down (even broke his vow of not keeping the bow once lifted) (1.46)

    Conclusion: Such a kind and softhearted person is fit to receive self-knowledge (1.46 purport)

    Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Classical
    Translation
    1.44 Sri Sankaracharya did not comment on this sloka. The commentary starts from 2.10.
    Śrī Rāmānujācārya Classical
    Translation
    1.26 - 1.47 Arjuna said - Sanjaya said Sanjaya continued: The high-minded Arjuna, extremely kind, deeply friendly, and supremely righteous, having brothers like himself, though repeatedly deceived by the treacherous attempts of your people like burning in the lac-house etc., and therefore fit to be killed by him with the help of the Supreme Person, nevertheless said, 'I will not fight.' He felt weak, overcome as he was by his love and extreme compassion for his relatives. He was also filled with fear, not knowing what was righteous and what unrighteous. His mind was tortured by grief, because of the thought of future separation from his relations. So he threw away his bow and arrow and sat on the chariot as if to fast to death.
    Śrī Abhinavagupta Classical
    Translation
    1.35 1.44 Nihatya etc. upto anususruma. Sin alone is the agent in the act of slaying these desperadoes. Therefore here the idea is this : These ememies of ours have been slain, i.e., have been take possession of, by sin. Sin would come to us also after slaying them. Sin in this context is the disregard, on account of greed etc., to the injurious conseences like the ruination of the family and the like. That is why Arjuna makes a specific mention of the [ruin of the] family etc., and of its duties in the passage 'How by slaying my own kinsmen etc'. The act of slaying, undertaken with an individualizing idea about its result, and with a particularizing idea about the person to be slain, is a great sin. To say this very thing precisely and to indicate the intensity of his own agony, Arjuna says only to himself [see next sloka]:

    Personal Guidance
    Tradition warns of long-term consequences — those who destroy dharmic structures suffer not in one life but across lifetimes.
    Practical Applications
    • Take seriously the long arc of karma; one moment of dharmic violation can echo for many lifetimes.
    • Consult senior Vaiṣṇavas before making decisions that affect family or community structures.
    • When you must make a decision with broad consequence, sit with it longer than feels comfortable.
    Reflection Questions
    • What decision am I about to make whose consequences I have not weighed seriously?
    • Whose elder voice should I be consulting before I act?
    Analogy

    *Aho bata* — "alas, how strange!" — is the speech of a man who has surprised himself with his own conclusions. Arjuna stands outside his own actions and sees them as a stranger would: "look at me, preparing a great sin." The capacity for such self-witness is already half the cure; the other half is the diagnosis the Gītā will provide.

    Important Words
    • apratīkāram — without being resistant
      *A-* (negation) + *prati-kṛ* (to act against, to oppose). "Non-resisting." The same syntactic logic as *ahiṁsā* (non-injury). Arjuna proposes *apratīkāra* as his stance — but the Gītā will distinguish *non-resistance under provocation* (a virtue in śānti circumstances) from *non-resistance in defence of dharma* (a vice, here).
    • aśastram — without being fully equipped
      *A-* + *śastra* (weapon). "Weaponless." Arjuna is proposing the classical ascetic / Jain image: to stand unarmed before the armed. A noble image when the path is *sannyāsa*; an evasion when the path is *kṣatriya-dharma*. The Gītā will later teach that one's *svadharma*, even if bloody, is superior to another's *paradharma*, even if peaceful (BG 3.35).
    • śastra - pāṇayaḥ — those with weapons in hand
      *Śastra* + *pāṇi* (hand) — "weapon-handed." Bahuvrīhi compound. Arjuna stages a tableau: he, weaponless; they, weapon-handed. The image is morally tilted by its very framing. The Gītā will reframe: he is not weaponless either — he has Gāṇḍīva *and* Kṛṣṇa as charioteer. Refusing the weapon is its own kind of pride.
    • kṣema - taram — better
      *Kṣema* — welfare, peace, security. Same root as in *yoga-kṣema* (BG 9.22: "I provide and preserve"). *Kṣema-tara* — comparative — *more peaceful*. Arjuna says his death would be *more conducive to welfare*. The Gītā will eventually take this very word and place it inside Kṛṣṇa's promise — *I* carry the *yoga-kṣema* of the devotee. Self-sacrificed *kṣema* is a poor substitute for surrendered *kṣema*.
    Better for me if the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, weapons in hand, were to kill me unarmed and unresisting on the battlefield.
    Purport

    It is the custom – according to kṣatriya fighting principles – that an unarmed and unwilling foe should not be attacked. Arjuna, however, decided that even if attacked by the enemy in such an awkward position, he would not fight. He did not consider how much the other party was bent upon fighting. All these symptoms are due to soft-heartedness resulting from his being a great devotee of the Lord.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    45. It would be better for me if the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, weapons in hand, were to kill me without weapons and without opposition.
    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    45. It would be better for me if the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, weapons in hand, were to kill me without weapons and without opposition.
    Commentary

    “Even if you are disinclined to fight, Bhīṣma and others are inclined to fight and will kill you. So what is to be done?” “Not opposing them will be my prāyaścitta for the sin of thinking of killing relatives. This is most beneficial (kṣemataram), removing sin just by this prāyaścitta at the end of life (when they kill me.) And Bhīsma and others will also not incur sin by killing me in this manner.”

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Better for me if the sons of Dhrtarastra, weapons in hand, were to kill me unarmed and unresisting on the battlefield. (cn/DS) To beg, for a ksatriya, is not part of his culture. And Arjuna is saying that is better for him to beg and suffer complete humiliation in this life then to have to kill all those kinsmen and then suffer all the reactions for all the sins that will make him suffer for thousands and thousands of years.

    Personal Guidance
    Arjuna would rather die than violate his sentiment — but dying for sentiment is not the same as dying for dharma.
    Practical Applications
    • Do not glorify renunciation that masks an unwillingness to act.
    • Test your own 'I would rather die than do that' statements — what is being protected, sentiment or dharma?
    • Ask Kṛṣṇa to remove the romance from your renunciations and leave only the substance.
    Reflection Questions
    • Which of my hard lines are dharmic, and which are merely dramatic?
    • Where am I willing to be 'killed' (criticized, lose status) just to avoid doing what is right?
    Analogy

    "Better for me to be killed unarmed" is the rhetoric of romance, not of dharma. There is a kind of moral grandstanding in offering one's life on terms one chooses; it can look like saintly non-resistance and yet be a refusal to enter the situation one's birth has placed one in. The Gītā will treat such offers with great gentleness — and with no acceptance.

    Important Words
    • saṅkhye — in the battlefield
      *Saṅkhya* — battle (here); but the same word, with another stress, names the philosophy of *sāṅkhya* (enumeration, analysis). Sanskrit lets the same letters mean *battle* and *analysis*. The chapter ends on a word that contains the next chapter's name: Sāṅkhya-yoga (BG 2). Vyāsa is preparing the transition phonetically.
    • upasthe — on the seat
      Locative of *upastha* — lap, seat. Arjuna sits down on the *seat* of the chariot — not on the ground, not in retreat. He stays *on* the chariot. The collapse is contained within the divine framework. He has not fled the war; he has only sat down on the platform from which the Gītā will be heard.
    • upāviśat — sat down again
      Aorist of *upa-viś* — to sit down. Same root *viś-* as in *praviśanti* and *viśvatomukha*. "He took his seat." The same verb the Vedic tradition uses for a disciple *taking his seat* before a teacher (*upaviṣat*). The military *upāviśat* is, by its very verb, also the disciplic *upaveśana* — sitting down to learn.
    • visṛjya — putting aside
      Absolutive of *vi-sṛj* — to release, to let go, to discharge. Same root as *sṛṣṭi* (creation, lit. "emission"). Arjuna *releases* his bow and arrows. The Gītā will use *visṛjya* repeatedly for the act of *renouncing*. The first *visṛjya* of the Gītā is a confused one. The last *visṛjya* (BG 18.66: *sarva-dharmān parityajya*) will be the perfected one.
    • śoka — by lamentation
      *Śoka* — grief, sorrow. The exact word Kṛṣṇa will name in His first teaching reply (BG 2.11: *aśocyān anvaśocas tvam* — "you grieve for those not worthy of grief"). The chapter ends on the word the next chapter will diagnose. *Śoka* is the disease; the Gītā is its medicine.
    Sañjaya said: Arjuna, having thus spoken on the battlefield, cast aside his bow and arrows and sat down on the chariot, his mind overwhelmed with grief.
    Purport

    While observing the situation of his enemy, Arjuna stood up on the chariot, but he was so afflicted with lamentation that he sat down again, setting aside his bow and arrows. Such a kind and soft-hearted person, in the devotional service of the Lord, is fit to receive self-knowledge. Thus end the Bhaktivedanta Purports to the First Chapter of the Śrīmad Bhagavad-gītā in the matter of Observing the Armies on the Battlefield of Kurukṣetra.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    46. Speaking in this manner, Arjuna, giving up his bow and arrows, mind disturbed with lamentation, sat down on his chariot amidst the warriors assembled for battle.
    Commentary

    Sitting on his chariot (rathopaṣṭhe) amidst the assembly of warriors (saṅkhye), Arjuna gave up his weapons.

    Thus the commentaries on the first chapter of the Gītā, Sārārtha Varṣiṇī, has been completed for giving joy to the hearts of devotees, following after the tradition of our ācāryas.

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    46. Speaking in this manner, Arjuna, giving up his bow and arrows, his mind disturbed with lamentation, sat down on his chariot amidst the war.
    Commentary

    “Then what happened?” Saṣjaya then replied with this verse. Arjuna sat down on the chariot in the midst of the battle. Previously he had been standing in order to fight, and to see the opposing army. From the first chapter it is understood that inquiry about ātmā takes place in a person who is compassionate in nature and non-violent, and not in one who is cruel and violent. Chapter 2

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Sanjaya said: Arjuna, having thus spoken on the battlefield, cast aside his bow and arrows and sat down on the chariot, his mind overwhelmed with grief. (cn/DS) Arjuna has put down his bow. And to understand how significant is this, he had vowed: "If anyone suggests me to put down this gandiva bow of mine, I vow I will kill him!" Here we can understand how heavy it was for Arjuna to take part in this battle against his own kinsmen.
    Study Notes — Gauranga Priya Dāsa
    Gauranga Priya Dāsa Study
    Bhakti-śāstrī Notes, ISKCON Chowpatty (2009)
    Theme

    Arjuna had vowed to kill anyone who even suggested that he put down his bow. An incident later

    tested that vow.

    During the battle, Karṇa defeated and severely injured Yudhiṣṭhira. Karṇa then taunted Yudhiṣṭhira,

    saying, “You are not even a kṣatriya! You should learn how to fight. See how easily I have defeated

    you! I’m not even going to bother to kill you.”

    When Arjuna heard of Yudhiṣṭhira’s injury, he immediately left the battlefield and went to Yudhi-

    ṣṭhira’s tent. Upon hearing that Arjuna had left the battlefield, Yudhiṣṭhira concluded that Arjuna,

    avenging his honor, had already killed Karṇa and had now come to inform him.

    But it wasn’t true. Arjuna had left the battlefield only out of concern for Yudhiṣṭhira’s injury.

    As soon as Yudhiṣṭhira saw Arjuna, he asked, “Have you killed Karṇa and avenged me?”

    Arjuna replied, “No, I did not kill Karṇa. I only came to see how badly you were hurt.”

    Yudhiṣṭhira was furious. He said, “You have left the battlefield without even killing Karṇa? You

    coward! How could you have done this? It is better that you give up your Gāṇḥīva bow!”

    Upon hearing his words, Arjuna became enraged and thought, “How dare Yudhiṣṭhira suggest that I

    give up my Gāṇḥīva bow, which is more dear to me than my life! I have vowed to kill anyone . . .”

    Arjuna drew his sword to slay his brother. Kṛṣṇa, who was watching, immediately caught Arjuna’s

    arm and said, “All right, you have to kill Yudhiṣṭhira. It is your vow, but kill him by insulting him. For

    a kṣatriya, an insult is worse than death.”

    As Yudhiṣṭhira sat there regretting his words to Arjuna,

    Arjuna angrily approached him and said, “You say I am a coward because I left the battlefield with-

    out killing Karṇa, but look what you have done. You looked on as our wife Draupadī was insulted. I

    would have alone killed the entire Kaurava army, but you would not allow me. You are not a man.

    You are not a king!”

    Arjuna finished hurling his insults at Yudhiṣṭhira, but then quickly touched Yudhiṣṭhira’s feet and

    begged forgiveness for his words.

    Arjuna had not lightly made his “Gāṇḥīva vow.” Therefore it is significant that Arjuna—the great

    son of Pāṇḥu and Indra—himself cast aside his bow and sat down on the chariot, his mind over-

    whelmed with grief. We can only imagine how disturbed Arjuna must have been about the disaster

    awaiting him and the entire world

    Classical Ācāryas
    Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Classical
    Translation
    1.46 Sri Sankaracharya did not comment on this sloka. The commentary starts from 2.10.
    Śrī Rāmānujācārya Classical
    Translation
    1.26 - 1.47 Arjuna said - Sanjaya said Sanjaya continued: The high-minded Arjuna, extremely kind, deeply friendly, and supremely righteous, having brothers like himself, though repeatedly deceived by the treacherous attempts of your people like burning in the lac-house etc., and therefore fit to be killed by him with the help of the Supreme Person, nevertheless said, 'I will not fight.' He felt weak, overcome as he was by his love and extreme compassion for his relatives. He was also filled with fear, not knowing what was righteous and what unrighteous. His mind was tortured by grief, because of the thought of future separation from his relations. So he threw away his bow and arrow and sat on the chariot as if to fast to death.
    Śrī Abhinavagupta Classical
    Translation
    1.26 - 1.47 Arjuna said - Sanjaya said Sanjaya continued: The high-minded Arjuna, extremely kind, deeply friendly, and supremely righteous, having brothers like himself, though repeatedly deceived by the treacherous attempts of your people like burning in the lac-house etc., and therefore fit to be killed by him with the help of the Supreme Person, nevertheless said, 'I will not fight.' He felt weak, overcome as he was by his love and extreme compassion for his relatives. He was also filled with fear, not knowing what was righteous and what unrighteous. His mind was tortured by grief, because of the thought of future separation from his relations. So he threw away his bow and arrow and sat on the chariot as if to fast to death. 1.46. It would be more beneficial for me if Dhrtarastra's men with weapons in their hands, should slay me, unresisting and unarmed. 1.46 If, on the contrary, the sons of Dhritarashtra, with weapons in their hand, should slay me, unarmed and unresisting, surely that would be better for my welfare!"
    Swami Sivananda Classical
    Translation
    1.46. If the sons of Dhritarashtra with weapons in hand should slay me in battle, unresisting and unarmed, that would be better for me.
    Commentary

    1.46 यदि if? माम् me? अप्रतीकारम् unresisting? अशस्त्रम् unarmed? शस्त्रपाणयः with weapons in hand? धार्तराष्ट्राः the sons of Dhritarashtra? रणे in the battle हन्युः should slay? तत् that? मे of me? क्षेमतरम् better? भवेत् would be.No Commentary.

    Swami Gambhīrānanda Classical
    Translation
    1.46 If, in this battle, the sons of Dhrtarastra armed with weapons kill me who am non-resistant and unarmed, that will be more beneficial to me.
    Shri Purohit Swami Classical
    Translation
    1.46 If, on the contrary, the sons of Dhritarashtra, with weapons in their hand, should slay me, unarmed and unresisting, surely that would be better for my welfare!"

    Personal Guidance
    The bow falls from the hand precisely so that Kṛṣṇa can be approached as guru — Arjuna's collapse is the necessary doorway into the rest of the Gītā.
    Practical Applications
    • Treat your moments of total collapse as Kṛṣṇa's invitation to formally take shelter.
    • When you cannot continue under your own steam, do not bandage yourself — surrender.
    • Read BG 2.7 immediately after this verse to feel the natural progression from collapse into surrender.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where has the bow fallen from my hand in this season of life?
    • Am I willing to use this collapse as a doorway to formally surrender to Kṛṣṇa?
    Analogy

    The bow falls. The arrows are laid aside. The warrior sits down on the seat of his own chariot — which is now, with Kṛṣṇa at its reins, no longer a war-chariot but a teaching-platform. The collapse is total, and exact: the *visṛjya* (laying aside) prepares the *prapadye* (taking shelter) that will come in 2.7.

    Stories
    Hanumān and the falling bow

    Hanumān, riding on the flag above the chariot, had agreed to remain there until the war was complete. When Arjuna's bow falls in this verse, the flag is still flying. The servant of Rāma is watching the descendant of Pāṇḍu collapse. Hanumān himself, in another age, had refused to despair even before Laṅkā with its hundred-thousand soldiers and golden walls. He had said: *I am the servant of Rāma; what is impossible for the Lord's servant?*

    Arjuna's collapse is the moment Hanumān's quiet presence on the flag becomes most pointed. The lineage of perfect service is silently overhead while the warrior of imperfect service sinks. The Gītā will now begin the work of bringing Arjuna into the same posture Hanumān has always held — and the bow that has just fallen will, by chapter 18, be picked up again in that very spirit.
